concepts.title: Approach to the medical patient
key_points: A medical patient's history usually tells you more than the physical exam does, which reverses the trauma priority
Scene size-up and the primary assessment come first regardless, and a medical call can still have an unsafe scene
The history of the present illness is gathered with OPQRST, the past history with SAMPLE
A responsive medical patient gets a history-focused assessment; an unresponsive one gets a rapid head-to-toe first
Pill bottles, the refrigerator, the room and the family are all part of the history
Reassess every 5 minutes for an unstable patient and every 15 for a stable one
misconceptions: Running a trauma-style rapid exam on a talking medical patient and learning nothing
Skipping the medication list because the patient 'takes a lot of things'
Treating an unresponsive medical patient as purely medical and missing an injury from a fall
exam_favorites: Why history outweighs exam in a medical patient
Which assessment path a responsive vs unresponsive medical patient gets

read.plain:
A medical patient is different from a trauma patient in one important way: the story matters more than what your hands find.

On a trauma call you look for damage. You expose, you palpate, you find the broken thing. On a medical call the broken thing is usually invisible. The information is in what the patient tells you, what their medications tell you, and what the room tells you.

So the order changes. For a responsive medical patient you take the history first and let it steer your exam. OPQRST for what is happening now, SAMPLE for the background. Then you examine what the history points at.

For an unresponsive medical patient you cannot take a history, so you do the opposite: a rapid head-to-toe, then vital signs, then whatever history you can get from family, from bottles on the counter, from a wallet card.

What does not change is the front of the call. Scene safety, standard precautions, general impression, primary assessment, life threats. A medical call can absolutely have an unsafe scene, and a patient who is short of breath still needs an airway checked before you ask about their history.

And look around. A refrigerator with insulin in it, a nebuliser on the table, an oxygen concentrator in the corner, a pile of dialysis supplies. That is history.
read.standard: The medical patient assessment inverts the emphasis of the trauma pathway: the history of present illness carries the greater diagnostic weight, with physical examination directed by that history rather than conducted comprehensively. Scene size-up, standard precautions and primary assessment remain unchanged and precede all else. For the responsive medical patient, OPQRST characterises the present complaint and SAMPLE establishes background, after which a focused examination targets the implicated system. For the unresponsive medical patient, a rapid head-to-toe survey and vital signs precede history, which is then obtained from bystanders, family, medication containers and medical identification. Environmental inspection is part of history-gathering. Reassessment occurs at five-minute intervals for the unstable patient and fifteen-minute intervals for the stable patient.

eli_new.analogy: On a trauma call you are a mechanic looking for the dent. On a medical call you are a detective taking statements.
eli_new.body: New EMTs run the same physical exam on everybody because it feels like doing something. On a medical patient who is talking to you, the exam is the smaller half of the job. Ask, listen, look at the room, and let what you hear decide what you touch.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assess a responsive medical patient and how that differs from an unresponsive one.

must_hit.point: Scene safety and primary assessment first regardless
Responsive: history first, OPQRST and SAMPLE, then focused exam
Unresponsive: rapid head-to-toe first, then history from others
The room and the medications are history
Reassess 5 minutes unstable, 15 stable

story.title: The refrigerator
story.dispatch: Medic 4 — 61-year-old female, generally unwell, no other information.
story.body:
She said she felt tired and a bit off and could not be more specific than that, and her vitals were unremarkable.

The student opened the refrigerator looking for somewhere to put the used sharps and saw a shelf of insulin pens.

She had not mentioned diabetes because nobody had asked, and she did not think of it as being related to feeling tired.

concepts.title: Common medical chief complaints
key_points: A chief complaint is what the patient says is wrong, in their words, not your impression of it
The common EMS medical complaints are chest pain, shortness of breath, altered mental status, abdominal pain, weakness, dizziness, syncope, nausea and vomiting
Vague complaints like 'weakness' or 'not feeling right' are associated with serious illness surprisingly often, especially in older patients
The same complaint can come from many systems, so the complaint starts the assessment rather than ending it
Document the complaint in the patient's own words in quotation marks
misconceptions: Rewriting the chief complaint as a diagnosis, for example recording 'anxiety attack' when the patient said they cannot breathe
Treating 'generalised weakness' as a low-acuity complaint
Assuming a complaint belongs to the obvious system
exam_favorites: Chief complaint in the patient's own words
Why vague complaints are high risk in older patients

read.plain:
The chief complaint is what the patient says is wrong. Not what you think is wrong. Their words, in quotation marks, on the report.

There is a reason to be strict about this. The moment you write down 'anxiety attack' instead of 'I can't breathe', you have made a diagnosis, and everybody downstream of you inherits it. The triage nurse reads your diagnosis instead of the patient's symptom.

The complaints you will see most are chest pain, shortness of breath, altered mental status, abdominal pain, weakness, dizziness, fainting, and nausea or vomiting.

One of those deserves particular attention: weakness. 'I just feel weak.' 'I'm not right.' It sounds like nothing. In an older patient it is associated with serious illness often enough that it should raise your index of suspicion rather than lower it. Heart attacks present as weakness. So does sepsis. So does a slow gastrointestinal bleed.

And remember that a complaint is a starting point, not a system. Abdominal pain can be cardiac. Shortness of breath can be metabolic. Weakness can be almost anything. The complaint tells you where to begin asking, not where to stop.
read.standard: The chief complaint is recorded as the patient's own stated reason for seeking care, quoted verbatim, and is distinguished from the provider's impression. High-frequency EMS medical complaints include chest pain, dyspnoea, altered mental status, abdominal pain, generalised weakness, dizziness, syncope and nausea or vomiting. Non-specific complaints, particularly generalised weakness in geriatric patients, correlate with serious underlying pathology at a rate that warrants a raised index of suspicion rather than a reduced one; acute coronary syndrome, sepsis and occult gastrointestinal haemorrhage all present this way. A chief complaint localises the initial line of questioning but does not establish the system of origin, and complaints frequently arise from a system other than the one implied.

eli_new.analogy: The chief complaint is the headline, not the article. It tells you which page to turn to.
eli_new.body: Writing down what the patient actually said feels less professional than writing a diagnosis. It is the opposite. The quote is data; your diagnosis is a guess, and if you write the guess, everybody after you reads the guess.

teach.prompt: Explain what a chief complaint is, how it is documented, and why vague complaints deserve attention.

must_hit.point: The patient's own words, quoted
Not the provider's diagnosis or impression

story.title: Just weak
story.dispatch: Medic 2 — 79-year-old male, generalised weakness, no pain.
story.body:
He had been feeling weak for two days. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, nothing that fitted a box.

The crew wrote down what he said, took a full set of vitals, and transported him without much urgency.

The complaint on the chart read 'generalised weakness x 2 days'. That was the right thing to write, and it was enough for the nurse to take him seriously.

concepts.title: Stroke: ischemic, hemorrhagic and TIA
key_points: A stroke is a loss of blood supply to part of the brain, and the deficit maps to the part that lost supply
Ischemic stroke is a blocked vessel and accounts for the large majority of strokes
Hemorrhagic stroke is a ruptured vessel, and is more often associated with sudden severe headache, vomiting and rapid deterioration
You cannot tell the two apart in the field, which is why the field job is recognition and rapid transport, not classification
A transient ischemic attack resolves completely but is a warning, not a false alarm, and is transported
Last known well is the single most important piece of history, because treatment eligibility is measured from it
Any stroke patient can lose their airway, so airway and positioning come before the stroke scale
Hypoglycemia mimics stroke closely enough that a blood glucose is part of every stroke assessment
misconceptions: Trying to decide ischemic versus hemorrhagic in the field
Standing down because the symptoms resolved, which is a TIA and still needs transport
Recording 'found this morning' instead of an actual last-known-well time
Assuming a patient who cannot speak cannot hear or understand you
exam_favorites: Ischemic versus hemorrhagic proportions and presentation

read.plain:
A stroke is the brain losing its blood supply. Which abilities disappear depends entirely on which part of the brain went without.

There are two mechanisms. Most strokes are ischemic: a clot blocks a vessel and everything downstream starves. A minority are hemorrhagic: a vessel ruptures and blood pushes into tissue that has nowhere to expand.

Hemorrhagic strokes are more likely to come with a sudden severe headache, vomiting, and a patient who gets worse quickly. But 'more likely' is not a field test. You cannot tell them apart at the kerbside, and you do not need to. Your job is recognising that this is a stroke and getting the patient to a place that can image the brain.

A transient ischemic attack is the same picture that then goes away completely. It is not a false alarm. It is a warning shot, and a meaningful number of people who have one go on to have a real stroke soon after. The patient goes to hospital.

The piece of history that matters most is last known well: the last moment somebody can testify this patient was at their normal baseline. Not when symptoms were noticed, and not when somebody woke up and found them. Treatment eligibility is measured from that moment, so get a time and get a name to go with it.

Two more things. Stroke patients lose airways, from weakness, from vomiting, from a drooping side of the mouth. Airway first, always. And check a blood glucose on every single one, because low blood sugar produces a stroke picture convincingly enough to fool people, and it is the one cause you can fix.
read.standard: Cerebrovascular accident results from interruption of cerebral perfusion, with deficits corresponding to the territory affected. Ischemic infarction, arising from thrombotic or embolic occlusion, constitutes the large majority of presentations; intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage constitute the minority and are associated more frequently with abrupt severe headache, emesis and rapid neurological deterioration. Field differentiation is not possible and is not attempted; prehospital management consists of recognition, airway protection, and expedited transport to a facility capable of neuroimaging. Transient ischemic attack denotes complete resolution of deficit and carries substantial short-term stroke risk, warranting transport. Time of last known well governs eligibility for time-dependent intervention and is the priority historical datum. Blood glucose measurement is mandatory in every suspected stroke, as hypoglycaemia reproduces focal neurological deficit and is correctable.

eli_new.analogy: A stroke is a power cut in one district of a city. Which lights go out tells you which district, not what caused it.
eli_new.body: The instinct is to work out what kind of stroke it is. Let go of that. In the field the two look alike often enough that guessing adds nothing and costs minutes. Recognise, protect the airway, check a sugar, get a last-known-well time, and move.

Hemorrhagic is a bleed, often with severe headache and rapid decline

story.title: Found this morning
story.dispatch: Medic 7 — 68-year-old female, weakness on one side, found by her husband.
story.body:
He found her at seven, slumped and unable to speak clearly, and called immediately.

The crew asked when he had last seen her normal. He said seven. They asked when she had gone to bed. He said about ten the night before, and she was fine then.

The last known well was ten at night, not seven in the morning, and that is a nine-hour difference that decides what the hospital can offer her.

rows.right: Often gradual over minutes to hours, sometimes sudden

rows.left: Focal — one side, one function, mapping to a brain territory
rows.right: Usually global — confusion, altered behaviour, though it can mimic a focal deficit
Often cool and diaphoretic
Low — this is the finding that separates them
Often rapid and dramatic improvement

rows.left: Recognise, airway, last known well, rapid transport
rows.right: Give glucose per protocol if the patient can protect their airway
A fixable cause that is missed if nobody checks a sugar

concepts.title: Stroke scales and last known well
key_points: A stroke scale is a structured way of finding a focal deficit quickly and reporting it in language the hospital recognises
The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale tests facial droop, arm drift and speech
FAST is Face, Arms, Speech, Time; BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes to catch posterior strokes that FAST misses
Any single abnormal finding is a positive scale — the patient does not need to fail every element
A negative scale does not exclude a stroke, particularly a posterior one
Last known well is a time and a witness, recorded together
Pre-notify the receiving hospital, because a stroke alert mobilises a team before you arrive
misconceptions: Requiring all three Cincinnati elements to be abnormal before calling it positive
Using FAST alone and missing a posterior stroke presenting as dizziness and imbalance
Recording when symptoms were discovered as the last known well time
Not pre-notifying because the hospital is close
exam_favorites: One abnormal finding is a positive scale
Last known well versus time discovered

read.plain:
A stroke scale exists so that a focal deficit gets found fast and described in words the hospital already understands.

The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale has three parts. Ask the patient to smile and watch for one side lagging. Ask them to hold both arms out with eyes closed and watch for one drifting down. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring or the wrong words.

FAST is the same idea packaged for the public: Face, Arms, Speech, Time.

BE-FAST adds two letters to the front, Balance and Eyes, and it exists because of a real gap. Strokes in the back of the brain do not always produce a drooping face or a drifting arm. They produce sudden severe dizziness, a patient who cannot walk straight, double vision. A pure FAST assessment walks past those.

Here is the part people get wrong: one abnormal finding makes the scale positive. You are not adding up a score and needing a majority. A drifting arm on its own is a positive scale.

And a negative scale does not clear anybody. If the history sounds like a stroke and the scale is clean, believe the history.

Last known well is a time plus a witness, written down together. 'Twenty-two hundred, per husband' is useful. 'This morning' is not.

Finally, call it in early. A stroke alert pulls a team, a scanner and a bed together before your wheels stop. Doing that from the truck is worth more than anything else you can do on the way.
read.standard: Prehospital stroke scales provide structured detection of focal neurological deficit and standardised communication. The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale assesses facial droop, arm drift and speech abnormality. FAST encodes Face, Arms, Speech and Time; BE-FAST prefixes Balance and Eyes, improving sensitivity for posterior circulation events which frequently lack the anterior findings FAST detects. A single abnormal element constitutes a positive scale; scoring thresholds are not applied. A negative scale does not exclude cerebrovascular accident, particularly posterior circulation stroke, and clinical suspicion based on history supersedes a negative scale. Time of last known well is documented together with the witness attesting to it. Prearrival notification activates institutional stroke pathways and is performed irrespective of transport distance.

eli_new.analogy: A stroke scale is a smoke detector, not a diagnosis. One beep is enough to act on, and silence does not prove there is no fire.
eli_new.body: Two mistakes get made constantly. The first is thinking you need all three Cincinnati findings — you need one. The second is trusting a clean FAST in a patient who suddenly cannot walk straight and is seeing double. That is what BE-FAST was invented for.

story.title: She just felt dizzy
story.dispatch: Medic 3 — 54-year-old female, dizziness and vomiting.
story.body:
Her face was symmetrical, her grip was equal, her speech was clear. FAST was negative three times.

She could not stand without falling to one side and she was seeing double, and the crew recorded dizziness and transported her without an alert.

It was a posterior stroke. Balance and Eyes are the two letters that would have caught it.

Eyes — sudden vision loss or double vision
Face — ask for a smile; watch for one side lagging
Arms — both arms out, eyes closed; watch for one drifting down
Speech — repeat a simple sentence; listen for slurring or the wrong words
Time — last known well, with the witness who attests to it. Pre-notify.

concepts.title: Seizures, status epilepticus and postictal care
key_points: A seizure is disordered electrical activity in the brain; a convulsion is one way that shows itself, not the only way
Generalised seizures involve the whole brain and impair consciousness; focal seizures start in one area and may or may not
During the seizure you protect the patient from injury and protect the airway — you do not restrain them and you put nothing in the mouth
Status epilepticus is a seizure that does not stop, or repeated seizures without recovery in between, and it is a true emergency
The postictal period is the recovery afterwards: confusion, drowsiness, sometimes agitation, gradually clearing
A postictal patient who is not gradually improving needs another explanation
Check a blood glucose on every seizure patient, because hypoglycemia causes seizures
A first-ever seizure, a seizure in pregnancy, a seizure in water, and a seizure with injury all raise the stakes
misconceptions: Putting something in the mouth to stop the tongue being swallowed — the tongue cannot be swallowed and objects break teeth and block airways
Restraining a convulsing patient, which causes injury without shortening the seizure
Assuming any confused patient after a seizure is simply postictal and needs no further thought
Not checking a glucose because the patient has a known seizure disorder
exam_favorites: What not to do during a convulsion
What the postictal period looks like and when it is not postictal

read.plain:
A seizure is the brain's electrical activity going out of order. The shaking everybody pictures is one way that shows itself. Plenty of seizures do not look like that at all.

Generalised seizures involve the whole brain at once and consciousness goes. Focal seizures start in one region; the patient may stay aware, or may not, and may just stare, or repeat a movement, or smell something that is not there.

While it is happening, your job is small and specific. Move furniture. Put something soft under the head. Protect the airway, turn them on their side if you can. Time it.

And two things you do not do. You do not restrain them, because you cannot stop the seizure by holding them and you will break something. And you do not put anything in their mouth. The old idea about swallowing the tongue is simply wrong — it is anatomically impossible — and objects put in mouths break teeth and end up in airways.

Status epilepticus is a seizure that will not stop, or seizures stacked back to back without the patient coming round in between. That is an emergency in the real sense. The brain is consuming oxygen it is not getting, and it needs medication an EMT does not carry. Recognise it, support the airway, and move.

Afterwards comes the postictal period. Confused, sleepy, sometimes combative, slowly clearing. The word 'slowly clearing' is the important part. A postictal patient gets better. One who is not getting better, or is getting worse, has something else going on and deserves a fresh look.

And check a sugar. Every time. Low blood glucose causes seizures, and a known seizure disorder does not protect anybody from also being hypoglycemic.
read.standard: Seizure denotes disordered cerebral electrical activity; convulsive motor activity represents one manifestation among several. Generalised seizures involve both hemispheres with impairment of consciousness; focal seizures originate in a discrete region with variable preservation of awareness, and may manifest as automatisms, sensory phenomena or behavioural arrest. Prehospital management during the ictal phase comprises protection from environmental injury, airway positioning and timing of the event. Restraint is contraindicated, as is insertion of any object into the oral cavity; tongue occlusion by swallowing is anatomically impossible and oral objects produce dental trauma and airway obstruction. Status epilepticus denotes continuous seizure activity or recurrent seizures without interictal recovery of consciousness and constitutes a time-critical emergency requiring pharmacological termination beyond EMT scope. The postictal phase is characterised by progressive resolution of confusion and somnolence; failure to improve, or deterioration, mandates evaluation for an alternative cause. Blood glucose measurement is indicated in every seizure presentation.

eli_new.analogy: A seizure is an electrical storm. You cannot stop the storm by holding the roof down; you clear the things it could knock over and wait for it to pass.
eli_new.body: Two reflexes to unlearn. The first is grabbing hold of someone who is convulsing — you will not shorten it and you may dislocate a shoulder. The second is putting something in their mouth. Nobody swallows their tongue. It is attached.

Do not restrain and do not put anything in the mouth
Status epilepticus is continuous or back-to-back seizures without recovery
Postictal is confusion that gradually clears

Check a blood glucose

story.title: Still not right
story.dispatch: Engine 9 — 34-year-old male, witnessed seizure, now conscious.
story.body:
Known epilepsy, missed doses, a witnessed convulsion lasting about a minute. Textbook.

Twenty minutes later he was no clearer than he had been at five minutes, and if anything he was harder to rouse.

Postictal patients get better. This one was not getting better, and the crew stopped calling it postictal.

concepts.title: Syncope
key_points: Syncope is a brief loss of consciousness from a transient drop in cerebral perfusion, with spontaneous full recovery
The recovery is the distinguishing feature: a syncopal patient comes round and is oriented, unlike a postictal patient
Causes divide roughly into cardiac, neurologic, and everything else — and the cardiac ones are the dangerous group
Syncope during exertion, syncope with no warning at all, and syncope in a patient with cardiac history are the concerning patterns
Vasovagal syncope usually has warning: light-headedness, nausea, a hot flush, visual greying
Anyone who has fainted may also have been injured by the fall, particularly the head
Orthostatic vital signs may be taken per protocol, but a patient who faints on standing does not need them repeated to prove it
misconceptions: Treating all fainting as benign because young people faint
Missing the head injury caused by the fall
Confusing syncope with a seizure when there were a few jerks at the end, which can happen with a simple faint
Letting a patient refuse transport after exertional syncope
exam_favorites: What distinguishes syncope from a postictal state
The injury caused by the fall

read.plain:
Syncope is fainting, described properly: consciousness lost briefly because the brain's blood supply dipped, followed by a full spontaneous recovery.

That recovery is the thing that separates it from a seizure. A patient who has fainted comes round and knows where they are, usually within a minute. A patient who has seized is confused for a good deal longer. If somebody is still muddled twenty minutes later, you are not looking at a simple faint.

Causes sort into a few piles. The common, benign pile is vasovagal: standing too long, a fright, blood, pain, heat. These usually come with a warning — going light-headed, feeling sick, vision greying at the edges, a wave of heat — and the patient often has time to sit down.

Then there is the pile that worries you: cardiac. A rhythm that stopped supplying the brain for a few seconds. These are the ones that kill people, and there are patterns that point at them. Fainting during exertion rather than after it. Fainting with no warning whatsoever, straight from normal to the floor. Fainting in someone with a known cardiac history or a family history of sudden death.

If any of those are in the story, this patient is going to hospital, and their reluctance is not the deciding factor.

And whatever the cause: they fell. From standing, usually onto something hard, with no hands out to break it because they were unconscious on the way down. Check the head. Check the face. People get discharged from faints and come back with a bleed.

One more thing that catches people out. A simple faint can produce a few jerks of the limbs at the end. That is not a seizure.
read.standard: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness secondary to global cerebral hypoperfusion, with spontaneous and complete recovery. Rapid return to full orientation differentiates syncope from the postictal state. Aetiologies are conventionally grouped as cardiac, neurologic and other, of which cardiac causes carry the greatest mortality. Features suggesting cardiac origin include syncope occurring during exertion, absence of any prodrome, and known cardiac or family history of sudden death. Vasovagal syncope typically features a prodrome of light-headedness, nausea, diaphoresis and visual greying. Brief myoclonic jerking may accompany uncomplicated syncope and does not indicate seizure. All syncopal patients sustain an uncontrolled fall and require assessment for traumatic injury, particularly head injury. Orthostatic vital signs may be obtained per protocol.

eli_new.analogy: A faint is the brain briefly losing its water pressure. Lying down restores it, which is why fainting fixes itself.
eli_new.body: The trap is that fainting is so common and so often harmless that it gets waved through. Two questions cut through it: was there any warning, and were they exerting themselves? No warning, or during exercise, and this stops being a simple faint.

story.title: On the pitch
story.dispatch: Medic 1 — 17-year-old male, collapsed during a football match, now alert.
story.body:
He was up before anyone reached him, embarrassed, saying he was fine and it was just the heat.

He had gone down mid-sprint, with no warning, and his uncle had died suddenly at forty-one.

Exertional syncope, no prodrome, family history. Three flags in one story, and none of them are visible on the patient standing in front of you looking well.

concepts.title: Headache red flags
key_points: Most headaches are not emergencies, so the field task is spotting the few that are
A sudden headache that reaches maximum intensity almost immediately is the single most concerning story
A headache described by the patient as the worst of their life is treated as significant whatever their headache history
Headache with fever and a stiff neck raises the possibility of a central nervous system infection and prompts precautions
Headache with any focal neurological deficit, seizure, or altered mental status is a neurological emergency until proven otherwise
Headache after a head injury, particularly in an anticoagulated or older patient, is significant even when the injury looked minor
Headache that wakes the patient from sleep, or is worse on straining, or is new in someone over 50, are further flags
Field care is supportive: airway, positioning, dim and quiet, minimal handling, and transport
misconceptions: Dismissing a headache because the patient has migraines
Treating 'worst headache of my life' as dramatic language
Bright lights and loud handling for a patient who is photophobic
Missing the fever and neck stiffness because the complaint was recorded as headache
exam_favorites: Headache with fever and neck stiffness
Headache after a head injury on anticoagulants

read.plain:
Almost every headache you go to is not an emergency. The job is finding the ones that are, and there is a short list of stories that should make you sit up.

The first and most important is the sudden one. Not a headache that built up over an hour — one that arrived at full strength almost instantly, like a switch. Ask directly: did it come on gradually, or was it at its worst straight away? That single question is worth more than everything else you will ask about a headache.

Second, the words 'worst headache of my life'. People say it. Believe it. It matters even — especially — in somebody who gets headaches all the time, because they are the ones qualified to rank it.

Third, headache with fever and a stiff neck. That combination raises the possibility of an infection around the brain and spinal cord, and it changes what you wear as well as where you go.

Fourth, headache with anything neurological attached: a weak side, a change in speech, a seizure, confusion, a new visual problem. That is no longer a headache call.

Fifth, headache after a head injury. If the patient is older, or on a blood thinner, the injury does not need to have looked impressive. A minor bump plus anticoagulation is a combination that produces slow bleeds.

And a few more worth knowing: a headache that wakes someone from sleep, one that gets worse on coughing or straining, and a genuinely new type of headache in a patient over fifty.

What you actually do is unglamorous and matters more than it sounds. Airway, position of comfort, lights down, voices down, handle them gently, and go. A patient with a severe headache is often desperately light- and sound-sensitive, and a quiet, dim, smooth ride is real treatment.
read.standard: The majority of headache presentations are benign; prehospital assessment is directed at identifying the minority requiring urgent evaluation. Thunderclap onset — maximal intensity attained within seconds — is the most significant historical feature and is elicited by direct questioning about the speed of onset. Headache with fever and nuchal rigidity raises concern for central nervous system infection and prompts appropriate precautions. Additional concerning features include headache waking the patient from sleep, exacerbation on Valsalva, and new-onset headache in a patient over fifty. The student asked whether it built up like her usual ones. She said no — it was there all at once, while she was washing up, and it was the worst she had ever had.

The fact that she got headaches was exactly what made her able to say that.

concepts.title: Altered mental status and the AEIOU-TIPS differential
key_points: Altered mental status is a finding, not a diagnosis — it always has a cause and the cause is what you are looking for
AEIOU-TIPS is a structured differential: Alcohol, Epilepsy/Electrolytes, Insulin, Overdose/Oxygen, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric/Poisoning, Stroke/Shock/Seizure
The reversible causes an EMT can actually affect are low oxygen and low blood glucose, so both are checked on every altered patient
AVPU describes the level; the differential explains it — record both
A patient who smells of alcohol may also be hypoglycemic, head injured, or septic, and the smell explains nothing on its own
Airway is the first concern in any patient with a reduced level of consciousness
Establish the baseline: family telling you this is not how they normally are is diagnostic information
misconceptions: Stopping at 'intoxicated' and looking no further
Failing to check a glucose because a cause seems obvious
Recording AVPU and calling that an assessment of mental status
Assuming a nursing home patient's confusion is their baseline without asking
exam_favorites: The two reversible causes an EMT can find and treat
Why the smell of alcohol explains nothing

read.plain:
Altered mental status is not a diagnosis. It is a finding, like a fever. Something caused it, and the whole job is working out what.

AEIOU-TIPS is the list people use so they stop guessing and start working through possibilities.

A is alcohol. E is epilepsy, and electrolytes. I is insulin — meaning blood sugar, high or low. O is overdose, and oxygen. U is uremia, kidney failure poisoning the blood. T is trauma. I is infection. P is psychiatric, and poisoning. S is stroke, shock, and seizure.

It is not elegant and the letters do double duty, but it makes you consider a sepsis or a low sugar in a patient you had already written off as drunk.

Of everything on that list, two causes are both common and things an EMT can actually find and fix: low oxygen and low blood glucose. So both get checked on every altered patient. A pulse oximeter and a glucometer, every time, no exceptions and no judgment calls.

Record the level and the cause separately. AVPU tells you how deep it is. The differential is what you think is behind it. 'Responds to voice' is not an assessment of mental status; it is one line of one.

Now the big one. A patient smells of alcohol. Everybody in the room, including you, has already decided. And the smell of alcohol tells you exactly one thing: they have been drinking. It does not tell you they are not hypoglycemic. It does not tell you they did not hit their head when they went down. It does not tell you they are not septic. People die of head injuries in the corner of rooms because they smelled of drink.

Airway first, always. Reduced consciousness means a reduced ability to protect the airway.

And ask what normal looks like. 'She's a bit confused' means nothing until somebody who knows her tells you whether that is new. Family saying 'this is not her' is diagnostic information, and it is free.
read.standard: Altered mental status constitutes a clinical finding requiring aetiological investigation rather than a diagnosis. The AEIOU-TIPS mnemonic structures the differential: Alcohol; Epilepsy and Electrolytes; Insulin, denoting dysglycaemia; Overdose and Oxygen; Uremia; Trauma; Infection; Psychiatric and Poisoning; Stroke, Shock and Seizure. Hypoxia and hypoglycaemia represent the reversible aetiologies within EMT scope and are assessed in every presentation by pulse oximetry and blood glucose measurement. Level of consciousness, documented by AVPU, is recorded separately from the presumed aetiology. The presence of ethanol odour carries no exclusionary value and coexists with hypoglycaemia, traumatic brain injury and sepsis. Airway assessment and protection precede all other intervention where consciousness is reduced. Determination of the patient's cognitive baseline from family or carers constitutes essential diagnostic information.

eli_new.analogy: Altered mental status is the check engine light. AEIOU-TIPS is the list of things to look at before you decide it is nothing.
eli_new.body: The thing that kills patients here is the shortcut. Drunk, diabetic, demented, psychiatric — pick a label early and stop looking. The discipline is: check a sugar, check a saturation, ask what normal looks like, and only then start forming an opinion.

concepts.title: Diabetes physiology: insulin and glucose
key_points: Glucose is the fuel; insulin is the key that lets glucose into cells
Without insulin, glucose piles up in the blood while the cells starve in the middle of plenty
The brain is the organ that suffers first and worst, because it cannot store fuel and cannot use an alternative quickly
Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so insulin must be given
Type 2 diabetes: insulin is made but the body responds poorly to it; it is managed with oral medication, lifestyle, and sometimes insulin
Blood glucose falls when the patient takes their medication and does not eat, or exerts themselves unusually, or is unwell
Blood glucose rises with illness, infection, missed medication, and stress
misconceptions: Believing the cells have plenty of fuel whenever blood glucose is high
Thinking type 2 diabetics never take insulin
Assuming a diabetic patient's problem is always their diabetes
exam_favorites: Insulin as the key, glucose as the fuel
What makes glucose fall and what makes it rise

read.plain:
Glucose is the fuel every cell runs on. Insulin is the key that lets it through the door.

That one image explains most of what you need. If there is no key, glucose cannot get into the cells. It stays in the bloodstream, and the blood glucose reading goes up and up while the cells themselves are starving. Full fuel tank, no way to reach the engine.

The brain feels this first. It cannot store fuel for later, and unlike muscle it cannot switch quickly to burning something else. Which is why blood sugar problems announce themselves as brain problems: confusion, odd behaviour, a reduced level of consciousness, seizures. A patient acting strangely is a patient whose brain is not being fed properly, and low blood sugar is one of the commonest reasons for that.

Two types. In type 1, the pancreas has stopped producing insulin, so it has to come from outside. In type 2, insulin is being produced but the body has stopped responding to it well. Type 2 is managed with tablets and diet, and often with insulin too as time goes on — so do not assume that a patient on insulin is type 1.

What pushes the sugar down: taking the medication and then not eating, unusual exertion, alcohol, and being unwell enough to skip meals.

What pushes it up: infection, illness of any kind, missed medication, and physical stress. This catches people out. A diabetic with the flu often runs high, not low, because being ill raises the demand.

And hold onto this: a diabetic patient can have anything anyone else can have. Diabetes is a reason to check a glucose on every call. It is not a reason to stop thinking once you have.
read.standard: Glucose constitutes the primary cellular energy substrate; insulin facilitates cellular glucose uptake. Absent adequate insulin activity, serum glucose accumulates while intracellular glucose availability falls, producing cellular starvation despite hyperglycaemia. The central nervous system is affected earliest and most severely, lacking significant glycogen storage and the capacity for rapid substrate switching; consequently dysglycaemia manifests neurologically as confusion, behavioural change, reduced consciousness or seizure. Type 1 diabetes mellitus reflects absolute insulin deficiency requiring exogenous replacement. Type 2 reflects insulin resistance with relative deficiency, managed by oral agents, lifestyle modification and frequently exogenous insulin; insulin use therefore does not indicate type. Hypoglycaemia is precipitated by medication taken without adequate intake, unaccustomed exertion, alcohol and intercurrent illness reducing intake. Hyperglycaemia is precipitated by infection, intercurrent illness, omitted medication and physiological stress.

eli_new.analogy: Insulin is the key to the door. Glucose can be piled up outside the house and the people inside will still starve if nobody has the key.
eli_new.body: The counter-intuitive bit is that a high blood sugar reading does not mean the cells have fuel. It means the opposite: the fuel is stuck outside them. That is why a patient can be starving cellularly with a glucose reading through the roof.

concepts.title: Hypoglycemia: presentation and oral glucose
key_points: Hypoglycemia is the true emergency of the two, because the brain is being starved right now
Onset is usually rapid — minutes to an hour — compared with the days of a hyperglycemic crisis
The picture is confusion, odd or aggressive behaviour, sweating, pallor, tremor, hunger, and a rapid pulse; it can progress to seizure and unresponsiveness
Cool sweaty skin in a confused diabetic is the classic combination
It is regularly mistaken for drunkenness, a psychiatric episode, or a stroke
Oral glucose is given only to a patient who is awake enough to swallow and protect their own airway
Nothing is put in the mouth of a patient who cannot protect their airway — that patient needs a route an EMT does not have, so transport and call for a paramedic

read.plain:
Of the two blood sugar emergencies, this is the one that will hurt someone in front of you. A high sugar is a crisis that builds over days. A low sugar is a brain being starved right now.

It comes on fast: minutes to an hour. And it produces a picture that is easy to recognise once you have seen it and easy to misread if you have not.

The patient is confused. They may be behaving oddly, or aggressively, or in a way completely unlike themselves. Their skin is cool and sweaty and pale, they may be trembling, they may say they are hungry, and their pulse is fast. Left alone it goes on to seizures and unresponsiveness.

Cool sweaty skin in a confused diabetic is the combination worth memorising.

And here is where patients get hurt: this looks like other things. It looks like drunkenness. It looks like a psychiatric crisis. It looks like a stroke. Every one of those has been written on a chart for a patient who simply needed sugar. This is the reason a glucometer comes out for every altered patient, without exception.

Treatment is oral glucose, and there is exactly one condition attached: the patient has to be awake enough to swallow and protect their own airway. Can they hold a conversation? Can they follow the instruction to swallow? Then they can have it.

If they cannot — if they are unresponsive, or barely rousable, or having a seizure — then nothing goes in their mouth. Not gel, not juice, not sugar under the tongue. It will end up in their lungs. That patient needs glucose by a route you do not have, so the answer is airway management, transport, and a paramedic intercept if one is available.

When it works it works quickly, and it is genuinely one of the most satisfying things you will do. Recheck the glucose afterward. And ask why it happened — a patient who went low for a reason they cannot explain still needs to be seen.
read.standard: Hypoglycaemia constitutes the more time-critical of the dysglycaemic emergencies, reflecting acute cerebral substrate deprivation. Onset is typically rapid, over minutes to approximately one hour, contrasting with the subacute course of hyperglycaemic crises. Clinical features comprise altered mental status, behavioural disturbance including aggression, diaphoresis, pallor, tremor, hunger and tachycardia, progressing to seizure and unresponsiveness if untreated. Cool diaphoretic skin with confusion in a known diabetic is characteristic. Misattribution to intoxication, psychiatric illness or cerebrovascular accident is common and constitutes the principal source of preventable harm. Oral glucose administration requires intact airway protective reflexes and the ability to swallow; administration to a patient unable to protect the airway is contraindicated owing to aspiration risk, and such patients require airway management, transport and advanced-level intervention. Post-treatment glucose measurement and evaluation of the precipitating cause are indicated.

eli_new.analogy: A low sugar is the brain running out of petrol on the motorway. Everything about the patient's behaviour is an engine misfiring, not a personality.
eli_new.body: The single most important habit in this whole module: a glucometer comes out for every altered patient. Not the ones who look diabetic. Every one. Because low sugar wearing a costume — drunk, aggressive, psychiatric, stroke — is how people get missed.

concepts.title: Hyperglycemia, DKA and HHS
key_points: Hyperglycemia builds over hours to days, not minutes, so the patient has usually been unwell for a while
The classic early story is the three polys: passing large volumes of urine, extreme thirst, and excessive hunger
Those patients are profoundly dehydrated, because the glucose drags water out with it into the urine
Diabetic ketoacidosis happens when cells with no usable glucose burn fat instead and produce acid as a by-product
DKA gives deep sighing respirations — the body blowing off acid — and a sweet or fruity smell on the breath
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is the other crisis: extremely high glucose with profound dehydration but without the ketones and acid, more often in older type 2 patients
Skin is warm, dry and flushed, the opposite of the hypoglycemic patient
Field care is airway, oxygen as indicated, position, and transport — the treatment is fluid and insulin, neither of which is an EMT's
misconceptions: Expecting a rapid onset like hypoglycemia
Mistaking deep sighing respirations for respiratory distress and treating the breathing
Missing how dehydrated these patients are because they are not bleeding
Assuming a high sugar is less urgent than a low one and slowing down accordingly
exam_favorites: Deep sighing respirations and fruity breath in DKA
Why these patients are volume depleted

read.plain:
A high blood sugar crisis is a slow one. Hours to days, not minutes. By the time you are called, the patient has usually been getting steadily worse for a while and somebody has finally decided it is not going to sort itself out.

The early story is three things that all begin with poly-. Passing enormous volumes of urine. Being desperately thirsty. Being very hungry. The urine comes first: when there is too much glucose in the blood, the kidneys spill it, and glucose in the urine drags water out with it. The thirst is the body chasing the water it is losing. The hunger is those starving cells asking for fuel they cannot use.

Which means these patients are dry. Seriously, sometimes dangerously dry, and it is easy to underestimate because nothing is visibly leaking.

Now the two crises.

Diabetic ketoacidosis. The cells cannot use glucose, so they burn fat instead, and burning fat produces acid. The blood turns acidic and the body tries to correct it the only fast way it can — by breathing it off. That gives the deep, sighing, laboured-looking respirations that are so easy to mistake for a breathing problem. It is not a breathing problem. It is the compensation, and it is keeping them alive. The acid by-products also give the breath a sweet or fruity smell, sometimes described as like nail varnish remover.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is the other one. The glucose goes extraordinarily high and the dehydration is profound, but there is just enough insulin activity to stop fat being burned, so there is no acid and no ketones. It tends to be older type 2 patients, and it comes on even more slowly. They present confused and very dry.

The skin is warm, dry and flushed. Remember it as the mirror image of the cool, sweaty hypoglycemic patient.

And what do you do? Airway, oxygen if indicated, a position that lets them breathe, and transport. The treatment these patients need is fluid and insulin, and neither one is yours. That is not a small role — recognising this and moving is the whole contribution — but do not stand on scene looking for something to give.
read.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises develop over hours to days. The classical prodrome comprises polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia; osmotic diuresis secondary to glycosuria produces substantial volume depletion. Diabetic ketoacidosis arises when absent insulin activity forces lipolysis for energy, generating ketoacids and metabolic acidosis. Respiratory compensation manifests as deep, sighing Kussmaul respirations, frequently misinterpreted as primary respiratory distress; ketone excretion produces a sweet or acetone-like breath odour. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state features extreme hyperglycaemia and profound dehydration without significant ketosis, occurring predominantly in older patients with type 2 diabetes and developing more insidiously. Integument is characteristically warm, dry and flushed, opposite to the hypoglycaemic presentation. Prehospital management comprises airway maintenance, supplemental oxygen as indicated, positioning and transport; definitive therapy is fluid resuscitation and insulin, both beyond EMT scope.

eli_new.analogy: The kidneys start bailing out sugar, and the sugar takes the water with it. The thirst and the enormous volumes of urine are the same event seen from two ends.
eli_new.body: The trap here is the breathing. A DKA patient breathing deeply and hard looks like a respiratory emergency, and the instinct is to treat the breathing. That breathing is the only thing holding their blood chemistry together. Support it, do not try to slow it down.

concepts.title: Thyroid and adrenal emergencies
key_points: These are rare, and the EMT task is recognising that something endocrine may be happening rather than naming it
An overactive thyroid crisis presents with fever, a very fast heart rate, agitation or confusion, and warm sweaty skin
An underactive thyroid crisis presents at the other end: cold, slow, drowsy, with slow breathing and low body temperature
Adrenal crisis presents with weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, and shock that does not respond as expected to the usual measures
The history is the strongest clue: a patient on long-term steroid medication who becomes unwell, or who has recently stopped taking it, is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise
A patient on steroids who is unwell, injured or stressed may need more steroid, not less, and stopping abruptly is dangerous
Field care is supportive: airway, oxygen as indicated, temperature management, position, and transport
misconceptions: Trying to name the specific endocrine disorder in the field

exam_favorites: The steroid history as the key clue
Shock that does not respond as expected

read.plain:
These are rare, and nobody expects an EMT to diagnose them. What is expected is that you notice something does not fit, and that you take the medication history seriously.

The thyroid sets the body's metabolic pace. Too much and everything runs fast and hot: fever, a racing heart, agitation, confusion, warm sweaty skin, sometimes a patient who looks like they are in a severe panic but with a genuinely high temperature. Too little and everything runs slow and cold: drowsy, slow pulse, slow shallow breathing, cold to touch with a low body temperature, progressing to unresponsive.

The adrenal glands sit above the kidneys and produce the hormones that let the body cope with stress, including holding blood pressure up. When they fail, or when somebody who has been taking steroids for a long time suddenly stops, the body loses the ability to respond to stress at all. That looks like weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, and shock — and the shock has an unusual quality. It does not respond the way you expect it to.

Here is the practical part, and honestly the only part you must carry away. Look at the medication list. A patient on long-term steroids who has become unwell, been injured, or has recently stopped or run out of their medication is at risk of an adrenal crisis. That patient needs more steroid, not less, and abruptly stopping is genuinely dangerous. If the list has a steroid on it and the patient is unwell out of proportion to what you can see, say so on your handover.

Everything you do is supportive. Airway, oxygen as indicated, do something about their temperature in either direction, position them sensibly, and go.
read.standard: Thyroid and adrenal emergencies are uncommon; prehospital recognition rather than specific diagnosis is the objective. Thyrotoxic crisis presents with hyperpyrexia, marked tachycardia, agitation or delirium and warm diaphoretic skin. Myxoedema crisis presents conversely with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, somnolence and progressive obtundation. Adrenal crisis manifests as weakness, emesis, abdominal pain and shock refractory to expected response. Pharmacological history is the principal diagnostic indicator: patients on long-term corticosteroid therapy who become unwell, sustain injury, or abruptly discontinue therapy are at risk, requiring increased rather than decreased steroid provision; abrupt cessation is hazardous. Prehospital management is supportive, comprising airway maintenance, supplemental oxygen as indicated, temperature management, positioning and transport.

eli_new.analogy: The thyroid is the thermostat and the adrenals are the emergency generator. One breaks by running too hot or too cold; the other breaks by failing to start when it is needed.
eli_new.body: You will not diagnose these and you are not meant to. What you are meant to do is read the medication list. Long-term steroids plus an unwell patient equals a sentence you say out loud at handover, and that sentence is the entire EMT contribution.

concepts.title: Allergic reaction versus anaphylaxis
key_points: An allergic reaction is the immune system overreacting to something harmless; anaphylaxis is that reaction affecting the whole body at once
The line between them is not how bad the rash looks — it is whether the airway, breathing or circulation is involved
Skin findings alone, however dramatic, are an allergic reaction
Airway swelling, wheeze or stridor, hypotension, or sudden collapse make it anaphylaxis
Gastrointestinal symptoms — cramping, vomiting, diarrhoea — alongside skin findings after an exposure also point to anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis can occur with no skin findings at all, which is how it gets missed
The distinction matters because it decides whether epinephrine is indicated
A patient's sense that something is very wrong, or a feeling of impending doom, is a real finding
misconceptions: Grading severity by how much rash there is
Waiting for hives before calling it anaphylaxis
Treating throat tightness as anxiety
Assuming a reaction that started mild will stay mild

read.plain:
An allergic reaction is the immune system deciding that something harmless is a threat and mounting a response out of all proportion. Anaphylaxis is that same response going body-wide and starting to close things down.

Here is the distinction that matters, and it is not the one people instinctively use. It is not how dramatic the rash is. Someone can be covered head to foot in hives and be having an allergic reaction. Someone else can have no rash whatsoever and be in anaphylaxis.

The question is whether the airway, breathing or circulation is involved.

Airway: swelling of the lips, tongue, throat; a hoarse voice; a feeling that the throat is closing; stridor. Breathing: wheeze, tightness, difficulty getting air. Circulation: low blood pressure, dizziness, pallor, collapse.

Any of those, after an exposure, is anaphylaxis.

There is a fourth thing worth adding. Gut symptoms — sudden cramping, vomiting, diarrhoea — appearing with skin findings after an exposure is also treated as anaphylaxis. The gut is smooth muscle and it reacts too.

Now the dangerous version. Anaphylaxis with no skin findings at all. Perhaps a third of cases have little or no rash, and those are the ones that get called asthma, or a panic attack, or food poisoning. If someone was exposed to something and is now struggling to breathe or going pale and faint, the absence of hives means nothing.

The reason all of this matters is that it decides one thing: whether epinephrine is indicated. That decision is why we are so precise about the line.

And take the patient's own alarm seriously. Patients in anaphylaxis often describe a feeling that something is terribly wrong, before anything measurable has changed. It is a recognised finding, not nerves.
read.standard: Allergic reaction denotes an exaggerated immune response to an otherwise innocuous antigen. Anaphylaxis denotes a systemic, multi-organ manifestation of that response. Differentiation rests on involvement of airway, breathing or circulation rather than the extent of cutaneous findings; isolated cutaneous manifestations, irrespective of severity, constitute allergic reaction. Airway involvement comprises oropharyngeal or laryngeal oedema, hoarseness, throat tightness and stridor; respiratory involvement comprises bronchospasm with wheeze and dyspnoea; circulatory involvement comprises hypotension, presyncope and collapse. Gastrointestinal involvement — cramping, emesis, diarrhoea — concurrent with cutaneous findings following exposure also satisfies anaphylaxis criteria. A substantial minority of anaphylactic presentations lack significant cutaneous findings, constituting the principal source of missed diagnosis. The distinction determines the indication for epinephrine. Patient-reported sense of impending doom is a recognised clinical finding.

eli_new.analogy: An allergic reaction is a fire alarm going off in one room. Anaphylaxis is the whole building's sprinkler system triggering at once, and the building is the patient.
eli_new.body: Unlearn the idea that severity is measured in rash. A covered-in-hives patient who is breathing fine and talking normally is having an allergic reaction. A patient with no rash at all who is going quiet and pale is in anaphylaxis, and is far closer to dying.

key_points: Epinephrine is the treatment for anaphylaxis, and delay in giving it is the thing most associated with deaths
It works by tightening blood vessels to restore pressure, relaxing the airways, and reducing swelling
The auto-injector is given into the outer thigh muscle, and can be given through clothing

read.plain:
Epinephrine is the treatment. Not an adjunct, not something to consider — the treatment. And the single finding that comes up again and again when anaphylaxis deaths are examined is that it was given late.

It does three things at once, and each one addresses part of what is killing the patient. It tightens blood vessels, which brings the blood pressure back up. It relaxes the airways, which opens up the wheeze. And it reduces the swelling that is closing the throat.

Giving it is mechanically simple. Outer thigh, into the muscle, and through clothing is fine — do not waste time undressing anybody. Hold the device in place for however long its instructions specify, because pulling it out early means part of the dose stays in the device. Then massage the site if your protocol says to.

Know your own scope here, because it varies. In some systems an EMT assists a patient with their own prescribed auto-injector and can do nothing else. In others the service carries them and the EMT administers. Find out which applies to you before you need to know.

In true anaphylaxis there is no absolute contraindication. Not age, not heart disease, not high blood pressure. The reaction will kill the patient faster than the epinephrine will hurt them. This matters because hesitation is what harms people here.

Afterwards, keep watching. The improvement can be remarkable and it can also wear off, and a patient who looks well ten minutes later can deteriorate again. One dose does not end the emergency.

The rest goes alongside: high-flow oxygen, rapid transport, and position. A hypotensive anaphylaxis patient lies flat, legs up if your protocol allows, unless their breathing will not tolerate it. Do not sit them up because it seems kinder, and do not let them walk to the ambulance. Sudden position changes in a patient with no blood pressure reserve have caused arrests.

And the used device is a sharp. Straight into the container.
read.standard: Epinephrine constitutes definitive prehospital therapy for anaphylaxis; delayed administration is the factor most consistently associated with fatal outcome. Mechanism comprises alpha-mediated vasoconstriction restoring perfusion pressure, beta-mediated bronchodilation, and reduction of mucosal oedema. Auto-injector administration is intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh, through clothing where necessary, held for the duration specified by the device, with site massage per protocol. Scope varies by jurisdiction between assisting with a patient's prescribed device and administering from service supply; providers must establish which applies. No absolute contraindication exists in genuine anaphylaxis. Continuous reassessment following administration is mandatory, as clinical improvement may be transient. Adjunctive management comprises high-concentration oxygen, supine positioning with leg elevation per protocol in hypotensive patients unless respiratory compromise precludes it, and expedited transport. Ambulation and sudden postural change are avoided. Used devices are disposed of as sharps.

eli_new.analogy: Epinephrine does three jobs at once: it squeezes the pipes, opens the airways and takes the swelling down. All three are the things trying to kill the patient.
eli_new.body: The killer here is hesitation. Everyone worries about giving epinephrine to an older patient or someone with a heart condition. In real anaphylaxis that worry is backwards — the reaction is the immediate threat, and the people who die are the ones who got it late.

concepts.title: Common allergens and biphasic reactions
key_points: The common triggers are foods, insect stings, medications, and latex
Nuts, shellfish, eggs, milk and wheat account for a large share of food reactions
The route matters less than people expect: a severe reaction can follow eating, injection, or contact
A biphasic reaction is a second wave hours after the first has settled, without any further exposure
That second wave is the reason every anaphylaxis patient is transported, even if they feel completely well
Previous mild reactions do not predict mild future ones — each exposure is its own event
Ask what was eaten, taken, touched or stung, and how long before symptoms started
Bring the packaging, the device, or the medication with you where practical
misconceptions: Reassuring a patient that because past reactions were mild this one will be
Allowing a refusal after anaphylaxis because the patient feels better
Assuming a reaction needs a swallowed allergen

exam_favorites: What a biphasic reaction is and why it drives transport
Past reactions do not predict future severity

read.plain:
Most reactions come from a short list. Foods — particularly nuts, shellfish, eggs, milk and wheat. Insect stings, especially bees and wasps. Medications, including antibiotics and common painkillers. And latex, which matters in healthcare settings and for anybody with repeated exposure.

The route matters less than people assume. Swallowed, injected, or touched can all produce a severe reaction. A patient does not have to have eaten anything.

Now the thing that governs your decisions: biphasic reactions. In some patients the reaction settles, they feel genuinely better, and then hours later a second wave arrives with no further exposure at all. It can be as severe as the first. It can be worse.

That is why every anaphylaxis patient goes to hospital, even the ones sitting up feeling fine and embarrassed. They need observation for a period their doctors will decide. Somebody who feels better and goes home is exactly the person a second wave catches, and often somewhere without help.

There is a related idea that catches people out. Previous mild reactions do not predict mild future ones. A patient who has had itchy lips twice before can have full anaphylaxis on the third exposure. Nothing about past events makes this one safer, so do not let a reassuring history slow you down.

History-taking here is quick and specific. What was eaten, taken, touched or stung? How long between the exposure and the first symptom? Has this happened before, and what happened that time? Do they carry an auto-injector, and has it been used today?

And take the evidence with you. The food packaging, the used device, the medication box. The hospital will want to know what caused this, and the answer is usually still in the room.
read.standard: Common allergens comprise foods — predominantly tree nuts, peanuts, shellfish, egg, milk and wheat — hymenoptera venom, pharmaceuticals including antibiotics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, and latex. Route of exposure does not reliably predict severity; ingestion, parenteral exposure and contact may each produce systemic reaction. Biphasic anaphylaxis denotes recurrence of symptoms following apparent resolution, occurring hours after the initial episode without re-exposure, and may equal or exceed the initial reaction in severity. This phenomenon mandates transport and observation of all anaphylaxis patients irrespective of apparent recovery. Severity of prior reactions does not predict severity of subsequent reactions. History should establish the agent, the interval to symptom onset, prior reaction history and auto-injector use. Causative packaging, devices or medications should accompany the patient where practicable.

eli_new.analogy: A biphasic reaction is the second wave after a tsunami. The water going back out is not the end of it, and people who walk back onto the sand are the ones who get caught.
eli_new.body: The single practical consequence of this whole concept: never let an anaphylaxis patient stay home because they feel better. Feeling better is what happens between the two waves.

concepts.title: Routes of exposure
key_points: There are four routes: ingestion, inhalation, injection and absorption through skin or mucous membrane

read.plain:
Poisons get in four ways: swallowed, breathed in, injected, or absorbed through skin and mucous membranes. That sounds like trivia. It is not — the route decides how fast it acts, and it decides what you have to do first.

Swallowed is the slowest, because the substance has to be absorbed from the gut. That delay is why a patient who took something twenty minutes ago can look completely well and still be in serious trouble. Do not be reassured by a well-looking patient early after an ingestion.

Inhaled and injected are the fast ones. Inhaled substances cross into the blood at the lungs almost immediately. Injected ones are already there.

Absorption is the one with a particular trap. If the substance is still on the skin, the exposure is still happening. Every minute it stays on is more dose. Which makes removing clothing and washing the patient an actual treatment with an actual clock on it, not housekeeping to be done once the important things are finished.

Now the part that matters most to you personally. An inhalation scene is a scene that can take you as well. A patient collapsed in a grain silo, a chemical store, a plant room, an enclosed space of any kind — whatever dropped them is still there, and it does not care that you have a uniform on. Do not enter. That is not caution, it is arithmetic: rescuers who go in become patients, and now nobody is being helped.

So: stop the exposure, and protect yourself while doing it. Those are the first two actions in every poisoning, in that order.

Then five questions, and get them in the order you can. What was it? How much? When? By what route? And what has anybody already done about it — has someone made them vomit, given them milk, tried something they read online?

And take the container. Always take the container.
read.standard: Toxic exposure occurs by four routes: ingestion, inhalation, injection and dermal or mucous membrane absorption. Route determines onset kinetics and the requisite initial intervention. Ingestion produces the slowest onset owing to gastrointestinal absorption, and early well-appearance does not exclude significant ingestion. Inhalation and injection produce the most rapid onset, the former by pulmonary absorption and the latter by direct parenteral delivery. Dermal absorption continues while the agent remains in contact, rendering decontamination a time-critical therapeutic intervention rather than an ancillary task. Inhalational exposure scenes present a hazard to responders; entry without appropriate atmospheric monitoring, respiratory protection and training is contraindicated, as rescuer incapacitation converts a single-patient incident into a multiple-casualty one. Initial priorities are cessation of exposure and responder protection. History should establish the agent, quantity, elapsed time, route and any interventions already undertaken. Containers should accompany the patient.

eli_new.analogy: The route is the tap. You can treat the flooding all you like, but until somebody turns the tap off you are just mopping.
eli_new.body: One rule that has killed more rescuers than any other: if a patient is collapsed in an enclosed space and you do not know why, the reason is probably still in there. It is not cowardice to stay out. It is the only way anybody gets helped.

read.plain:
The opioid overdose has a picture so consistent it is worth memorising as one item. Reduced level of consciousness. Slow or stopped breathing. Pinpoint pupils. Three findings, one diagnosis.

Now the most important sentence in this concept: what kills an opioid overdose patient is the breathing. Not the drug. The drug switches off the drive to breathe, and the patient dies of hypoxia while the opioid sits there doing nothing else particularly harmful.

That single fact sets your priority, and it is not the one people reach for. Ventilate first. Bag-valve mask, good seal, adequate rate, chest rising. You can fix the lethal problem with a piece of equipment you already have in your hand, before any drug comes out of any bag.

Naloxone reverses it by knocking the opioid off its receptors. It works, and it can be spectacular. At EMT level it is typically intranasal or by auto-injector, depending on your protocol.

But it has a property you have to plan around: it can wear off before the opioid does. The opioid is still in the body. When the naloxone fades, the patient can slide straight back into respiratory depression, and if that happens somewhere without a bag-valve mask, they die on the second round.

That is why every patient who receives naloxone is transported. Every one. Including — especially — the person who sat up, feels fine, is embarrassed and wants you to leave. Feeling fine is a snapshot, and the drug is still in them.

One more practical thing. Reversal can be abrupt and unpleasant. A patient who has just been pulled out of an opioid effect can wake confused, frightened, unwell, sometimes angry, and occasionally swinging. That is not bad character; it is a physiological reaction to having something stripped off their receptors in seconds. Position yourself accordingly and treat them gently.

And with the stronger synthetic opioids, one dose may not hold. Repeat per protocol — and keep ventilating. Ventilation is the treatment throughout.
read.standard: Opioid toxidrome comprises the triad of central nervous system depression, respiratory depression or apnoea, and miosis. Mortality derives from respiratory failure and consequent hypoxia rather than direct toxicity; ventilatory support therefore constitutes the primary intervention and precedes pharmacological reversal. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist, displacing agonist from receptor sites. EMT-level administration is typically intranasal or by auto-injector per protocol. Naloxone half-life may be shorter than that of the ingested opioid, permitting recurrence of respiratory depression following initial reversal; consequently all patients receiving naloxone require transport irrespective of apparent recovery. Abrupt reversal may produce agitation, distress or combativeness, and withdrawal phenomena. High-potency synthetic opioids may require repeat administration per protocol, with ventilatory support maintained throughout.

eli_new.analogy: Naloxone knocks the opioid off the receptor like someone taking your seat. The problem is that naloxone gets up before the opioid has left the building.
eli_new.body: The instinct is to reach for the naloxone, because it is the dramatic intervention. Resist it for thirty seconds. A patient who is not breathing needs air, and you have air in your hands right now. Bag first, then reverse.

concepts.title: Stimulants, sedatives and alcohol
key_points: Stimulants speed everything up: fast pulse, high blood pressure, dilated pupils, hot dry or sweating skin, agitation, paranoia
The dangers of stimulant toxicity are hyperthermia, seizures, and cardiac events in people too young to expect them
Sedatives slow everything down: drowsiness, slurred speech, poor coordination, slow shallow breathing, reduced consciousness
Sedatives combined with alcohol are far more dangerous than either alone, because both depress breathing
Acute alcohol intoxication is a sedative overdose and is treated as one, not as a behaviour problem

read.plain:
Three groups, and the first two are opposites.

Stimulants speed the body up. Fast pulse, high blood pressure, big pupils, skin that is hot and either dry or pouring with sweat, and a patient who is agitated, talkative, sometimes frankly paranoid. Three things kill them: overheating, seizures, and cardiac events in people far too young for cardiac events. Take a temperature if you can — hyperthermia in stimulant toxicity is a genuine emergency and it gets overlooked because everybody is focused on the behaviour.

Sedatives do the opposite. Drowsy, slurred, uncoordinated, breathing slowly and shallowly, sliding down the levels of consciousness. Same principle as opioids: the problem is the breathing, and the airway is your job.

Where sedatives become lethal is in combination with alcohol. Both depress breathing, and together they do it far more than either alone. A quantity of either that would have been survivable becomes fatal in combination. When you take the history, specifically ask what else — and specifically ask about alcohol, which people do not volunteer as a drug.

Which brings us to alcohol itself. Acute intoxication is a sedative overdose. Treat it as poisoning, because it is. A heavily intoxicated patient can lose their airway, aspirate, and die, and the fact that it is a familiar and socially ordinary poison does not change the physiology.

Withdrawal deserves its own attention, because it surprises people: it can be more dangerous than being drunk. A dependent drinker who stops — sometimes simply because they were admitted somewhere and could not get any — can develop tremor, sweating, agitation, hallucinations and seizures. Severe withdrawal has a real mortality rate.

Two habits for every intoxicated patient. Check a glucose. And look for an injury and for another explanation, because intoxicated people fall, get hit, and get ill just like everybody else — and the smell of drink is the most effective camouflage there is.

Finally, restraint. Sometimes necessary, never casual. The specific danger is positional asphyxia: a patient restrained face down, or folded forward, who cannot expand their chest. Never restrain anybody prone. Keep them where you can see their face and their breathing, and never stop monitoring them because they are restrained.
read.standard: Stimulant toxicity produces tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, hyperthermia with variable diaphoresis, agitation and paranoid ideation; principal mortality derives from hyperthermia, seizure and cardiac events in otherwise young patients. Sedative-hypnotic toxicity produces somnolence, dysarthria, ataxia, hypoventilation and progressive obtundation, with airway compromise as the primary threat. Concurrent sedative and ethanol ingestion produces additive respiratory depression substantially exceeding either agent alone. Acute ethanol intoxication constitutes sedative overdose and is managed as toxicological rather than behavioural presentation. Ethanol withdrawal may exceed intoxication in severity, producing tremor, diaphoresis, agitation, hallucinosis and seizures, with appreciable mortality in severe cases. Blood glucose measurement and assessment for traumatic injury and alternative pathology are indicated in every intoxicated presentation. Physical restraint carries significant risk; prone restraint is contraindicated owing to positional asphyxia, and restrained patients require continuous monitoring.

eli_new.analogy: Stimulants turn the engine up until something breaks. Sedatives turn it down until it stops. Alcohol is a sedative that nobody counts as one.
eli_new.body: Two things get missed constantly. The first is a temperature on an agitated stimulant patient — everyone watches the behaviour and nobody notices they are cooking. The second is that alcohol is a drug, so when you ask what they took and they say 'nothing, just drink', that is an answer that changes your management.

When the crew asked specifically about tablets, one of them remembered he had taken something to help him sleep earlier in the evening because he had been anxious about the party.

Either one alone he would probably have slept off. The two together were why he was not breathing properly.
