concepts.title: Carbon monoxide and cyanide
key_points: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does, so the blood stops carrying oxygen even though the lungs work perfectly
A pulse oximeter cannot tell carbon monoxide apart from oxygen, so a normal reading means nothing in a suspected exposure
The classic story is headache, nausea, dizziness and confusion in more than one person in the same building, often worse at home and better when out
The cherry-red skin described in textbooks is a late and unreliable finding — do not wait for it
Treatment is removal from the source and high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather
Cyanide interferes with the cells' ability to use oxygen at all, so the blood is loaded with oxygen the cells cannot touch
Cyanide is a genuine risk in enclosed-space fires because it comes off burning synthetic materials
A fire victim with soot, an altered mental status and a poor response to oxygen may have both poisonings at once
Any scene producing these gases can poison the crew, and the same rules about entry apply
misconceptions: Trusting a normal pulse oximeter reading in a suspected carbon monoxide exposure
Waiting for cherry-red skin before suspecting it
Treating only the burns in a fire victim and overlooking the inhaled poisons
Sending a patient back into the building that poisoned them
exam_favorites: Why pulse oximetry is useless in carbon monoxide exposure
Multiple people in the same building

read.plain:
Two poisons that both attack oxygen, at different points in the chain.

Carbon monoxide attacks transport. It binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does — by a wide margin — so it occupies the seats oxygen needs. The lungs work perfectly, the chest rises, the patient breathes, and none of it arrives. They suffocate with air going in and out.

Now the piece of equipment that will lie to you. A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish haemoglobin carrying carbon monoxide from haemoglobin carrying oxygen. It reads them the same. So a carbon monoxide patient can show you 99 percent while being profoundly poisoned. Normal saturation in a suspected exposure is not reassurance; it is a meaningless number, and if you treat it as reassurance it will cost you the diagnosis.

What should make you suspect it is the story. Headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion, flu-like without a fever. And especially: more than one person in the same building feeling the same way. Or symptoms that improve when the patient leaves home and come back when they return. That pattern is a boiler or a heater, and it is the single most useful thing you can elicit. Ask about the pets, too.

Forget the cherry-red skin. It appears late, appears inconsistently, and waiting for it means waiting too long.

Treatment is simple and it works: get them out, and high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather. Filling the blood with oxygen at high concentration drives the carbon monoxide off faster.

Cyanide is the other one, and it attacks the last step. It stops cells using oxygen at all. So the blood may be saturated, the transport working, and the cells still suffocating in the middle of plenty.

Where you will meet it is enclosed-space fires. Burning synthetic materials — furniture, foam, plastics, carpets — release it. A fire victim who is sooty, confused, and not improving the way you would expect on oxygen may have both poisonings running together. They frequently do.

And the obvious point that still needs saying: whatever is producing these gases will do the same to you. Same rule as every inhalation scene. Do not go in.
read.standard: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with affinity far exceeding that of oxygen, producing functional anaemia despite normal pulmonary function and normal arterial oxygen tension. Conventional pulse oximetry cannot differentiate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and yields falsely reassuring saturations; normal readings therefore carry no exclusionary value. Presentation comprises headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion and influenza-like symptoms without fever; simultaneous symptoms in multiple building occupants, or symptom improvement away from the premises, is highly suggestive. Cherry-red discolouration is a late and unreliable sign. Management comprises removal from source and high-concentration oxygen by non-rebreather mask, accelerating carboxyhaemoglobin dissociation. Cyanide inhibits cellular oxidative metabolism, producing cellular hypoxia despite adequate oxygen delivery, and is generated by combustion of synthetic materials in enclosed-space fires. Concurrent carbon monoxide and cyanide toxicity is common in fire victims presenting with soot, altered mental status and inadequate response to oxygen. Scene entry restrictions applicable to all inhalational exposures apply.

eli_new.analogy: Carbon monoxide takes the seats on the bus so oxygen cannot board. Cyanide lets the bus arrive full and then locks the doors of the building.
eli_new.body: The single fact to carry out of this concept: the pulse oximeter is useless here. It will show you a normal number on a patient who is being poisoned, and a crew that trusts the number goes home having missed it. Suspect it from the story, not from the machine.

Every one of them read between 98 and 100 percent on the pulse oximeter, and the newer crew member said so out loud as if it settled something.

It settled nothing. The oximeter cannot tell the two apart, and four people with headaches in one house is the actual finding.

concepts.title: Organophosphates and SLUDGEM
key_points: Organophosphates are found in agricultural and domestic pesticides and in nerve agents
They cause a flood of secretions from everywhere at once — the body wet on every surface
SLUDGEM captures it: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric upset, Emesis, Miosis
DUMBELS is the same picture by another list: Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhoea and Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation
What kills is the airway drowning in its own secretions, so suction and ventilation are the core treatment
Bronchorrhoea — the lungs filling with fluid the body is producing — is the specific lethal feature
The patient is contaminated and will contaminate you: gloves, gown, eye protection, and decontaminate before loading
Remove clothing, which holds the agent, and bag it
Antidotes exist but are outside EMT scope in most systems — know your protocol
misconceptions: Loading a contaminated patient into the ambulance without decontaminating first
Focusing on the pinpoint pupils and missing the airway filling up
Treating the vomiting rather than the breathing
Handling contaminated clothing without protection

read.plain:
Organophosphates are in pesticides — agricultural and domestic — and they are the chemistry behind nerve agents. Same mechanism, very different concentrations.

What they do is switch on secretion everywhere at once. Every gland and every wet surface goes into overdrive, and the patient is soaked from every direction simultaneously.

SLUDGEM is how it is remembered. Salivation — drooling, foaming. Lacrimation — streaming eyes. Urination. Defecation. Gastric upset — cramping. Emesis — vomiting. Miosis — pinpoint pupils.

DUMBELS is the same picture organised differently, and it earns its place because it names the thing that kills: Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhoea and Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

That B is the one to hold onto. Bronchorrhoea means the airways filling up with secretions the body itself is producing. The patient drowns from the inside, in fluid that keeps coming however much you remove. That is the lethal feature, and it means the treatment is airway, suction, and ventilation — relentlessly. Suction, ventilate, suction again. It is exhausting and it is the job.

Do not get distracted by the dramatic bits. The pinpoint pupils are a useful clue and do not threaten anybody. The vomiting and the diarrhoea are unpleasant and not the emergency. The lungs are the emergency.

Now protect yourself, because this patient is a hazard to you. The agent is on their skin and soaked into their clothing, and it absorbs through skin — yours as readily as theirs. Gloves, gown, eye protection at minimum. Get the clothing off, because clothing holds the agent and keeps dosing them. Bag it. And decontaminate before the patient goes in the ambulance, not after — a contaminated patient in a sealed metal box with you in it is a second casualty waiting to happen.

There are antidotes, and in most systems giving them is not an EMT function. Some services carry auto-injectors for responder self-protection. Know what your service carries and what your protocol permits before the day you need it.
read.standard: Organophosphate compounds occur in agricultural and domestic pesticides and constitute the chemical basis of nerve agents, producing cholinergic crisis through acetylcholinesterase inhibition. The resulting cholinergic excess produces generalised secretory overactivity, mnemonically captured as SLUDGEM: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastric upset, emesis and miosis. The alternative DUMBELS formulation — diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation — explicitly identifies bronchorrhoea, the principal cause of mortality. Copious airway secretion with bronchospasm produces death by airway flooding; management therefore centres on aggressive suctioning and ventilatory support. The patient constitutes a contamination hazard through dermal absorption; personal protective equipment comprising gloves, gown and eye protection is required, clothing must be removed and contained as it retains agent, and decontamination must precede transport. Antidotal therapy exists but generally falls outside EMT scope; providers must establish local protocol and service holdings.

eli_new.analogy: Every tap in the house turns on at once. The one that matters is the one running into the lungs.
eli_new.body: SLUDGEM is the famous mnemonic and DUMBELS is the useful one, because DUMBELS has the B in it. Bronchorrhoea is what kills these patients, and a mnemonic that leaves it out lets you concentrate on the pupils while the patient drowns.

concepts.title: Poison control and activated charcoal
key_points: Poison control centres give specific, current advice and should be contacted early, per protocol
Have the container, the substance name, the quantity, the time and the patient's weight ready before you call
Activated charcoal binds some swallowed substances in the gut so they are not absorbed
It is far less used than it once was, and where it is used at all it is time-limited and protocol-driven
It does not bind everything — alcohols, acids, alkalis, iron and lithium among others are not adsorbed
It is contraindicated where the airway is not protected, where the substance is a corrosive or a hydrocarbon, and where the patient cannot swallow
Inducing vomiting is not done, and syrup of ipecac is no longer used
Giving anything by mouth to a patient who may deteriorate creates an aspiration risk that has to be weighed
misconceptions: Inducing vomiting, or letting a family member who already has continue
Giving activated charcoal to a drowsy patient
Assuming charcoal works on every ingestion

read.plain:
Poison control centres are a genuine resource and an underused one. They hold current, specific information about substances you will never have heard of, and they will tell you what matters about the one in front of you. Contact them early, per your protocol, and if you can do it while moving, do it while moving.

Before you call, have your answers ready: the container itself if you have it, the name of the substance, roughly how much, what time, and the patient's weight. Those five things let them give you a real answer instead of a generic one.

Activated charcoal is the other half of this concept, and the honest summary is that it is used far less than it once was. The idea is sound — it binds certain substances in the gut so they are never absorbed — but the window is short, the benefit is narrower than was once believed, and the risk is real. Where it is still used it is tightly protocol-driven and time-limited.

Two things about it you must know.

It does not bind everything. Alcohols, acids, alkalis, iron, lithium — charcoal does nothing for these. Giving it for a substance it cannot bind achieves nothing and still carries every one of the risks.

And the contraindications are mostly about the airway. It is not given to a patient who cannot protect their own airway, cannot swallow, or is likely to deteriorate. It is not given for corrosives — acids and alkalis — because it does not help and it obscures the view when somebody needs to look at the damage. And it is not given for hydrocarbons, where vomiting it back up into the lungs is far worse than the original ingestion.

That aspiration risk is the whole of it. Charcoal in the lungs is a serious injury in itself. So the question before giving anything by mouth to a poisoned patient is: could this patient's consciousness drop in the next twenty minutes? If the answer is maybe, do not put anything in their mouth.

Lastly: do not make anybody vomit. Not with your finger, not with salt water, not with anything. Syrup of ipecac has been off the table for years. If a family member has already done it, note what came up, and stop them doing it again.
read.standard: Poison control centres provide substance-specific, current guidance and should be contacted early per protocol, ideally without delaying transport. Information required comprises the agent, quantity, elapsed time, patient weight and the container where available. Activated charcoal adsorbs certain ingested compounds within the gastrointestinal tract, preventing systemic absorption; contemporary use is substantially reduced, time-limited and protocol-governed. Charcoal does not adsorb alcohols, acids, alkalis, iron or lithium among other agents. Contraindications comprise unprotected airway, inability to swallow, anticipated deterioration in consciousness, corrosive ingestion — where it provides no benefit and obscures endoscopic assessment — and hydrocarbon ingestion, where aspiration risk exceeds ingestion risk. Pulmonary aspiration of charcoal constitutes a significant injury. Induced emesis is not performed and syrup of ipecac is obsolete.

eli_new.analogy: Charcoal is a sponge you send down after the spill. It only works on some spills, only if it gets there quickly, and only if the patient can be trusted to keep it down.
eli_new.body: The test question before giving anything by mouth to a poisoned patient is one sentence: could this person's consciousness drop in the next twenty minutes? If maybe, nothing goes in the mouth. Charcoal in the lungs is its own serious injury.

concepts.title: Toxidromes overview
key_points: A toxidrome is a pattern of findings that points at a class of substance when nobody can tell you what was taken
The four you should recognise are opioid, cholinergic, anticholinergic and sympathomimetic
Opioid: reduced consciousness, slow breathing, pinpoint pupils
Cholinergic: wet everywhere — SLUDGEM — with pinpoint pupils and secretions in the airway
Anticholinergic: the opposite — hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, agitated, retaining urine
Sympathomimetic: fast, hot, dilated pupils, high blood pressure, agitated — but sweating, which is what separates it from anticholinergic
Sweating is the discriminator between sympathomimetic and anticholinergic; pupils separate opioid from cholinergic
Mixed ingestions blur the patterns, so a toxidrome supports your thinking rather than closing it down
Vital signs including temperature and pupils are the assessment, and they are what make a toxidrome visible
misconceptions: Forcing a patient into one toxidrome when they have taken several things
Confusing sympathomimetic and anticholinergic because both are hot and agitated
Not taking a temperature and losing half the pattern
Treating the label instead of the airway and the vital signs

read.plain:
A toxidrome is a recognisable pattern of findings that tells you what class of substance you are dealing with when nobody in the room can or will tell you what was taken. Which is often.

There are four worth knowing properly.

Opioid. Reduced consciousness, slow or absent breathing, pinpoint pupils. Quiet and still. You know this one already.

Cholinergic — organophosphates and the like. Also pinpoint pupils, but the patient is wet from every orifice and surface, with secretions in the airway. SLUDGEM.

Anticholinergic. The exact mirror image of cholinergic. Dry as a bone, hot, red in the face, pupils wide open, agitated or hallucinating, and unable to pass urine. The old teaching rhyme captures it: hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter.

Sympathomimetic — stimulants. Fast pulse, high blood pressure, dilated pupils, hot, agitated, sometimes paranoid.

Now the two discriminations that actually earn you something.

Anticholinergic and sympathomimetic look almost identical at the bedside. Both are hot, both have big pupils, both are agitated, both have fast pulses. The separator is sweat. The sympathomimetic patient is drenched. The anticholinergic patient is bone dry — they cannot sweat, which is a large part of why they overheat. Put a hand on the skin. That is the test.

Opioid and cholinergic both give you pinpoint pupils. The separator is everything else: the opioid patient is dry and still, the cholinergic patient is soaked and producing fluid from everywhere.

Two cautions. First, mixed ingestions are extremely common, and someone who has taken three things will not present as any clean pattern. A toxidrome is a hypothesis, not an answer. If the patient does not fit, the patient is right and the pattern is wrong.

Second, and more important: treat the patient, not the label. Naming the toxidrome changes almost nothing you do at EMT level. Airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose and transport is the treatment whatever the pattern turns out to be. The value of recognising it is what you can hand over — 'this looks anticholinergic to me' is a genuinely useful sentence at the door.

Which is also why the vital signs matter so much here. A toxidrome is made of vital signs. Skip the temperature and you have lost a quarter of the picture.
read.standard: A toxidrome denotes a constellation of clinical findings suggesting a substance class where the ingested agent is unknown. Four principal patterns are recognised. Opioid toxidrome: central nervous system depression, respiratory depression, miosis. Cholinergic toxidrome: miosis with generalised secretory excess and bronchorrhoea, per SLUDGEM. Anticholinergic toxidrome: hyperthermia, anhidrosis, cutaneous flushing, mydriasis, agitation or delirium, and urinary retention. Sympathomimetic toxidrome: tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, hyperthermia, agitation with diaphoresis. Diaphoresis distinguishes sympathomimetic from anticholinergic presentations, which are otherwise closely similar; associated secretory findings distinguish cholinergic from opioid miosis. Polypharmacy ingestion is common and produces blurred or atypical patterns; toxidrome recognition informs but does not conclude assessment. Prehospital management at EMT level is determined by airway, breathing, circulation, temperature and glucose rather than by toxidrome identification; recognition primarily serves handover communication. Complete vital signs, including temperature and pupillary assessment, constitute the substance of toxidrome recognition.

eli_new.analogy: Four patterns, and the whole trick is a hand on the skin. Wet and fast is a stimulant. Dry and fast is an anticholinergic. Wet and slow with tiny pupils is cholinergic. Dry and slow with tiny pupils is an opioid.
eli_new.body: Do not spend energy naming the toxidrome and then forget to manage the patient. At your level the treatment is the same for all four: airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose, transport. Recognising the pattern is for the handover, and that is still worth doing.

concepts.title: Abdominal pain assessment and referred pain
key_points: The abdomen is assessed by quadrants, and the quadrant narrows what is underneath
OPQRST is the tool, and provocation and radiation carry most of the information
Visceral pain from hollow organs is dull, crampy and hard to point at; parietal pain from the lining is sharp and localised
A patient whose vague pain becomes sharp and localised has usually got worse, not better
Referred pain is felt somewhere other than the source — shoulder tip pain from blood or air under the diaphragm is the classic
Palpate the painful quadrant LAST, and watch the patient's face rather than your hands
Never assume abdominal pain is abdominal: a heart attack presents as epigastric pain often enough to matter
Nothing by mouth, position of comfort, and never apply heat
misconceptions: Palpating the painful area first and losing the rest of the exam
Assuming epigastric pain is indigestion
Giving a patient something to drink because they are thirsty

read.plain:
The abdomen is divided into four quadrants and the division does real work, because it tells you what is underneath your hand.

OPQRST is the framework, and two letters earn their keep here. Provocation — does movement make it worse? Someone who will not let the trolley go over a bump has a very different problem from someone who is writhing and cannot get comfortable. And radiation — where else does it go? That answer is sometimes the whole diagnosis.

There are two kinds of abdominal pain and knowing the difference is genuinely useful.

Visceral pain comes from the hollow organs themselves. It is dull, crampy, comes in waves, and the patient cannot point to it — ask them to and they will rub a whole region with a flat hand.

Parietal pain comes from the lining of the abdominal cavity being irritated. It is sharp, constant, and precisely locatable. Ask them to point and one finger lands on one spot.

Now the useful part: when the first becomes the second, the patient has got worse. Vague crampy pain all over that has become sharp pain in one place means something has progressed to involve the lining. That is a deterioration, and it is easy to mishear as improvement because the patient can now describe it clearly.

Referred pain is pain felt away from its source, because of how nerves are wired. The one to memorise is shoulder tip pain, which can mean blood or air under the diaphragm — from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, a bleeding spleen, or a perforation. A patient with abdominal pain and an aching shoulder tip with no shoulder injury is telling you something important.

On examination, one rule: palpate the painful quadrant last. Start furthest away and work towards it. If you go straight to the sore bit, the patient tenses up, and the rest of your exam is worthless. And watch their face, not your hands — the face tells you where the pain is more honestly than the words do.

One more thing, and it is the one that gets missed. Abdominal pain is not always abdominal. A heart attack can present as pain in the upper abdomen, particularly in older patients, in women, and in diabetics. Epigastric pain that came with sweating, nausea and shortness of breath is a cardiac presentation until proven otherwise.

And for management: nothing by mouth — they may go to theatre. A position of comfort, usually knees drawn up. No heat, ever, because it can make things worse.
read.standard: Abdominal assessment is organised by quadrant, localising the underlying viscera. OPQRST characterisation is applied, with provocation and radiation carrying particular diagnostic weight. Visceral pain, arising from hollow viscera, is dull, colicky and poorly localised; parietal pain, arising from peritoneal irritation, is sharp, constant and precisely localised. Transition from visceral to parietal character indicates progression rather than improvement. Referred pain denotes perception distant from the source; shoulder tip pain suggests subdiaphragmatic blood or air, as in ruptured ectopic pregnancy, splenic haemorrhage or viscus perforation. Palpation proceeds from the least painful quadrant to the most painful, with observation of facial response. Epigastric pain may represent acute coronary syndrome, particularly in geriatric, female and diabetic patients. Management comprises nil by mouth in anticipation of operative intervention, position of comfort, and avoidance of applied heat.

eli_new.analogy: Visceral pain is a wide flat hand rubbing a region. Parietal pain is one finger on one spot. When the hand becomes the finger, they got worse.
eli_new.body: The instinct is to go straight to where it hurts, because that is the interesting bit. Do the opposite. Go there last, or the patient guards and you learn nothing from anywhere else.

concepts.title: Peritonitis, appendicitis and bowel obstruction
key_points: Peritonitis is inflammation of the abdominal lining, and it produces a rigid, board-like abdomen the patient will not let you touch
A peritonitic patient lies very still with knees drawn up, because movement hurts — the opposite of colic
Appendicitis classically starts as vague pain around the navel and moves to the right lower quadrant over hours
Pain that becomes localised to the right lower quadrant with fever and vomiting is the pattern to recognise
Sudden relief of appendicitis pain can mean rupture, not recovery, and is followed by peritonitis

read.plain:
Three problems, all of them ultimately surgical, all of them recognisable from the way the patient lies and what the pain has done over time.

Peritonitis is inflammation of the abdominal lining. It comes from something leaking into a cavity that is meant to be sterile — a burst appendix, a perforated ulcer, infection. The abdomen becomes rigid and board-like, and the patient will not let you near it.

The posture is the giveaway. A peritonitic patient lies absolutely still, knees drawn up, and does not want the trolley to move. Every bump hurts. Compare that with colic, where the patient cannot get comfortable and is constantly shifting. Still means peritoneal. Writhing means colic. That single observation, made from the doorway, is worth a lot.

And once you have found a rigid abdomen, stop pressing on it. You have your finding. Confirming it three more times only hurts them.

Appendicitis has a story that is worth knowing because it is so characteristic. It starts as vague, hard-to-place pain around the navel. Over hours it migrates and settles in the right lower quadrant, and by then the patient can point at it. Fever, nausea and vomiting come along with it, and they usually do not want to eat.

The detail that catches people out: if that pain suddenly disappears, do not relax. Sudden relief can mean the appendix has ruptured and the pressure has released. The patient feels briefly better and is about to get very much worse, because peritonitis is what follows. A patient whose severe pain vanished on its own needs more attention, not less.

Bowel obstruction is different in character. The bowel is blocked and keeps trying to push past it, which produces crampy pain in waves. The abdomen distends. The patient vomits, sometimes enormous volumes, and in a long-standing obstruction the vomit can become faeculent — a finding nobody forgets. And nothing is passing: no stool, no gas.

Those patients get dry fast, because all that fluid is either being vomited out or sitting uselessly in dilated bowel. Watch for shock.

For all three: nothing by mouth, position of comfort, oxygen if indicated, monitor for shock, and transport. They need an operating theatre, and your job is to get them to one without making anything worse on the way.
read.standard: Peritonitis denotes peritoneal inflammation, typically from perforation or infection, producing involuntary guarding and board-like rigidity with marked tenderness. Characteristic posture is immobility with hips flexed, contrasting with the restlessness of colic; movement exacerbates peritoneal pain. Repeated palpation of a rigid abdomen is unnecessary once the finding is established. Appendicitis classically presents with periumbilical visceral pain migrating over hours to the right lower quadrant with localisation, accompanied by fever, nausea, vomiting and anorexia. Abrupt resolution of pain may indicate perforation with subsequent peritonitis rather than improvement. Bowel obstruction produces colicky pain, abdominal distension, vomiting which may become faeculent in established obstruction, and obstipation. Substantial third-space and vomitus fluid losses produce hypovolaemia. All three are surgical presentations: management comprises nil by mouth, position of comfort, oxygen as indicated, monitoring for shock and transport.

eli_new.analogy: A patient who lies rigidly still has peritonitis. A patient who cannot lie still at all has colic. You can make that call before you touch them.
eli_new.body: The appendicitis trap is the one to remember: pain that suddenly stops is not good news. Somebody who was in agony and is now comfortable has often just perforated, and the peace lasts about an hour.

concepts.title: Gastrointestinal bleeding
key_points: Upper GI bleeding comes from above the small bowel; lower GI bleeding from below it
Vomited blood may be bright red, or look like coffee grounds where it has sat in stomach acid
Black tarry stool means blood that has been digested on its way through, and it points upper

read.plain:
Gastrointestinal bleeding gets divided into upper and lower, and the dividing line sits at the top of the small bowel. That sounds academic until you realise it is exactly what the appearance of the blood tells you.

Blood that is vomited comes from the upper part. If it comes up fresh and fast it is bright red. If it has sat in stomach acid for a while it turns dark and granular, and the standard description — coffee grounds — is accurate enough that you will recognise it immediately.

Blood that has travelled the whole length of the gut gets digested along the way, and arrives as black, tarry, sticky stool with a smell people remember. That is an upper bleed too; it has just gone the long way round.

Bright red blood passed from below is usually a lower source. But be careful with that, because a very brisk upper bleed can move through fast enough to arrive still red. Bright red and a patient who looks terrible is a lot of blood moving quickly.

Now the sentence that matters most in this concept: what you can see tells you almost nothing about what has been lost. Most of it is still inside, in the bowel, where you cannot see it and neither can the patient. Crews get falsely reassured by a small amount in a bowl, and dangerously so.

So do not estimate volume. Assess for shock instead. Pulse first — rising rate is the early sign. Skin: pale, cool, sweaty. Mental status: anxious, then confused, then quiet. And blood pressure last, because it holds up until the patient has lost a great deal and then falls suddenly. A normal blood pressure in a bleeding patient is not reassurance, it is compensation.

Ask about three things specifically. Anticoagulants — blood thinners mean bleeding that will not stop on its own. Liver disease, which both causes bleeding and impairs clotting. And alcohol, for the same reasons plus the varices in the next concept.

Management is shock management. Airway with suction at hand and working, because these patients vomit and can aspirate. Oxygen as indicated. Keep them flat unless vomiting makes that impossible, and if it does, get them on their side rather than sitting up. Keep them warm — cold patients clot badly. Nothing by mouth. And go, because what they need is blood and an endoscopy, and those are at the hospital.
read.standard: Gastrointestinal haemorrhage is classified as upper or lower relative to the ligament of Treitz. Haematemesis indicates an upper source, appearing bright red with rapid bleeding or as coffee-ground material following exposure to gastric acid. Melaena — black, tarry, malodorous stool — reflects digested blood and also indicates an upper source. Haematochezia suggests a lower source, though brisk upper haemorrhage with rapid transit may present similarly. Visible blood loss correlates poorly with total loss, the majority remaining within the gastrointestinal lumen; assessment is therefore directed at shock findings rather than volume estimation. Tachycardia, cutaneous changes and altered mental status precede hypotension, which is a late finding reflecting decompensation. Anticoagulant therapy, hepatic disease and alcohol use exacerbate haemorrhage and impair haemostasis. Management comprises airway maintenance with suction immediately available, oxygen as indicated, supine positioning or lateral positioning where vomiting precludes it, active warming, nil by mouth and expedited transport.

eli_new.analogy: What you can see in the bowl is the tip of it. The rest is in a container you cannot look inside — which is why you read the patient, not the bowl.
eli_new.body: The single most dangerous habit here is being reassured by a small amount of visible blood. There is no relationship between what came out and what was lost. Read the pulse and the skin, and treat what they tell you.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis and pancreatitis
key_points: Both present as upper abdominal pain that an EMT manages the same way, so the task is recognition rather than distinction

read.plain:
These two get taught together because they present similarly, they sit next to each other anatomically, and at EMT level you manage them identically. So the goal is recognising a serious upper abdominal problem, not naming which one.

Gallbladder trouble gives right upper quadrant pain. The story is usually a meal, often a fatty one, an hour or two before it started. The pain can be severe and comes in waves, and the patient may be quite restless with it, because it is colicky rather than peritoneal. It sometimes refers to the right shoulder blade, which is worth knowing so you are not confused by a patient rubbing their back.

Pancreatitis is different in character. The pain sits high in the abdomen, often central, and it bores straight through to the back. Patients describe it as drilling or boring, and it tends to be constant and severe rather than coming in waves.

The posture is the useful finding. A pancreatitis patient usually wants to sit up and lean forward, or curl up on their side. What they do not want to do is lie flat, because flat makes it worse. So if you find someone with severe upper abdominal pain hunched forward who resists being laid down, let them stay there. Do not flatten a patient for the convenience of the trolley.

The two big associations for pancreatitis are alcohol and gallstones, which is part of why these two conditions keep company.

Both vomit, sometimes repeatedly, and both get dehydrated because of it. Look for that.

And care is exactly what it was for the last three concepts: nothing by mouth, a position of comfort chosen by the patient rather than by you, oxygen as indicated, watch for shock, and transport. There is nothing clever to do here, and the position of comfort is not a small thing — for a pancreatitis patient it is the only comfort available.
read.standard: Cholecystitis and pancreatitis present as upper abdominal pain with identical EMT-level management; recognition rather than differentiation is the objective. Biliary pain localises to the right upper quadrant, frequently follows ingestion of a fatty meal, is colicky in character with associated restlessness, and may refer to the right scapular region. Pancreatic pain localises to the epigastrium with penetration to the back, is typically constant and severe, and is characteristically relieved by sitting forward or lateral flexion and exacerbated by supine positioning. Principal associations of pancreatitis are alcohol use and cholelithiasis. Both produce repeated emesis with consequent dehydration. Management comprises nil by mouth, patient-selected position of comfort, oxygen as indicated, monitoring for shock and transport.

eli_new.analogy: Gallbladder pain arrives after dinner and comes in waves. Pancreatic pain bores through to the back and will not let the patient lie down.
eli_new.body: Do not spend effort deciding which one it is. You treat both the same way. The one thing that does change your behaviour is the posture: a pancreatitis patient who is sitting forward should be allowed to stay sitting forward.

key_points: Esophageal varices are swollen veins at the lower end of the food pipe, caused by back-pressure from liver disease
They can rupture and produce sudden, massive, bright red vomiting of blood
This is one of the few GI bleeds that can kill within minutes, and the immediate danger is the airway

read.plain:
Two groups of patients who are unusually fragile, for different reasons.

Esophageal varices first. Liver disease creates back-pressure in the veins that drain the gut, and that pressure forces blood into smaller veins that were never built for it — including a set at the bottom of the food pipe. They swell, they thin, and eventually one tears.

When that happens the bleeding is sudden, bright red, and enormous. This is one of very few gastrointestinal bleeds that can kill somebody in minutes, and it will not be the blood loss that does it first — it will be the airway. The patient is trying to breathe through a mouthful of blood while more arrives.

So your preparation is suction. Working, tested, in your hand. Not in the bag, not in the truck. If you are called to a known liver patient vomiting blood, get suction out before you are in the room, and think about how you would position someone whose airway is filling faster than you can clear it — usually on their side, head slightly down if your equipment and protocol allow it.

And their clotting is poor, because the liver makes the clotting factors and their liver is the problem. So this does not stop by itself. They need an endoscopy urgently, which means the useful things you can do are airway, oxygen, warmth and speed.

Dialysis patients are the second group. Their kidneys do not work and a machine does the job a few times a week. When they miss a session — through illness, transport failure, a bank holiday, or simply not going — two things build up: fluid and potassium.

Fluid overload is what you will see most. They become breathless, their ankles and legs swell, and they cannot lie flat. It looks a lot like heart failure, and the question that sorts it out is one line: when did you last dialyse? A breathless dialysis patient who missed Tuesday has told you the diagnosis.

Potassium rising is the dangerous one, because it causes fatal rhythm disturbances with very little warning. You cannot measure it, so treat any dialysis patient who has missed sessions as fragile and get moving.

Two practical rules about the fistula — the surgically joined artery and vein, usually in an arm, that the machine connects to. Never take a blood pressure on that arm. Never put anything in it. That fistula is how the patient stays alive, and clotting it off is a genuine harm. Use the other arm, always, and if both arms have one, ask.

And if a fistula site bleeds, it can bleed alarmingly, because it is arterial pressure in a vein. Direct pressure, firmly, and keep it there. Do not lift it every thirty seconds to see how it is doing.
read.standard: Oesophageal varices result from portal hypertension secondary to hepatic disease, producing dilated submucosal veins at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Rupture produces sudden massive haematemesis of bright red blood, constituting one of few gastrointestinal haemorrhages capable of causing death within minutes; the proximate threat is airway compromise rather than exsanguination. Management requires immediately available functioning suction, airway positioning, oxygen, warming and expedited transport. Coagulopathy secondary to hepatic synthetic failure prevents spontaneous haemostasis. Patients receiving haemodialysis present with distinct emergencies. Missed dialysis produces volume overload and hyperkalaemia. Volume overload presents with dyspnoea, peripheral oedema and orthopnoea, and is the commonest presentation; determining the interval since last dialysis is the key historical question. Hyperkalaemia produces potentially fatal dysrhythmia without reliable warning and cannot be assessed prehospitally. Arteriovenous fistulae must not be used for blood pressure measurement or vascular access; the contralateral limb is used. Fistula haemorrhage requires sustained direct pressure without intermittent release.

eli_new.body: Two rules that are absolute and easy to break under pressure: suction out before you walk in on a known liver patient vomiting blood, and never touch a fistula arm with a blood pressure cuff.

key_points: Kidney stone pain is severe, comes in waves, starts in the flank and radiates to the groin, and the patient cannot keep still

read.plain:
Three urinary problems, and each has one detail that changes what you do.

Kidney stones produce some of the worst pain in medicine. It starts in the flank, radiates down and forwards to the groin, and comes in waves as the stone moves. The patients are nauseated and often vomiting, and there is frequently blood in the urine.

The finding worth noticing is behavioural. A stone patient cannot keep still. They pace, they writhe, they change position constantly, they cannot get comfortable anywhere. That is genuinely useful, because it is the opposite of the peritonitis patient who lies rigid and still. Restless is colic; motionless is peritoneal.

Now the trap, and it is one that kills people. Flank pain in an older patient is not automatically a stone. A leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm presents exactly this way — flank or back pain, sometimes radiating to the groin — and if someone over about fifty has a first-ever episode of flank pain, particularly with any hint of shock, that possibility has to be in your mind and in your handover. A first stone at sixty-five is much less likely than a first stone at twenty-five.

Urinary tract infections in younger adults are straightforward: burning, going often, urgency, cloudy or offensive urine, sometimes low abdominal discomfort.

In older patients the whole thing changes. A urinary infection in an elderly person very commonly presents as confusion, or being off their feet, or just not being themselves — with no burning, no urgency, nothing urinary at all. This is one of the commonest causes of new confusion in older people, and it gets written off as dementia or as 'a bit muddled' constantly. If family tell you a confused older person is not normally like this, an infection is high on the list.

When infection reaches the kidney it adds fever, flank pain, rigors and feeling genuinely unwell, and from there it can progress to sepsis. Take vital signs seriously in anybody with a urinary infection and a fever.

Retention is the third. The patient cannot pass urine, the bladder keeps filling, and it becomes agonising. There is a firm, tender, distended swelling above the pubic bone. It sounds like a minor complaint on a dispatch card and it is one of the more painful things you will attend. Take it seriously, be gentle with the abdomen, and get them somewhere it can be relieved.
read.standard: Renal colic produces severe, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, accompanied by haematuria, nausea and vomiting. Motor restlessness is characteristic and contrasts diagnostically with the immobility of peritoneal irritation. Lower urinary tract infection presents with dysuria, frequency, urgency and cloudy or malodorous urine. In geriatric patients, urinary infection frequently presents as acute confusion or functional decline without urinary symptoms, constituting a common cause of new-onset delirium. Upper tract involvement adds fever, flank pain and systemic illness, with potential progression to sepsis. Urinary retention presents as inability to void with a progressively distended, tender suprapubic bladder and severe pain.

eli_new.body: The one that gets missed: an older person who is suddenly confused, with no urinary symptoms at all, may well have a urinary infection. The absence of burning proves nothing in that age group, and 'they're just getting confused' is a conclusion, not an assessment.

concepts.title: Renal failure and dialysis emergencies
key_points: Failing kidneys stop clearing waste, stop managing fluid, and stop regulating electrolytes
Acute kidney injury comes on over hours to days and is often reversible; chronic kidney disease is permanent and progressive
Dialysis does the job artificially, usually three times a week, and each session removes days of accumulated fluid and waste
The two emergencies around dialysis are missing it and complications of the session itself
Missing sessions causes fluid overload — breathlessness, swelling, unable to lie flat — and rising potassium, which causes fatal rhythms
Complications during or just after dialysis include low blood pressure, cramps, dizziness and collapse, from removing fluid too quickly
A dialysis patient who feels unwell just after a session has usually had too much fluid removed; one who feels unwell before it has usually had too little
The fistula rules apply absolutely: no blood pressure, no access, and firm sustained pressure if it bleeds

read.plain:
Kidneys do three jobs: clear waste, manage fluid balance, and keep electrolytes in range. When they fail, all three stop, and the consequences arrive in that order of visibility — you will see the fluid problem, you will not see the electrolyte problem until it kills someone.

There are two kinds of failure. Acute kidney injury develops over hours or days, often from dehydration, infection, shock or a medication, and it is frequently reversible if the cause is dealt with. Chronic kidney disease is permanent and gets slowly worse, and eventually reaches the point where the kidneys cannot sustain life without help.

That help is dialysis, usually three sessions a week, each taking hours. Each session pulls out several days' worth of accumulated fluid and waste. Understanding that rhythm explains almost every dialysis emergency you will attend, because the emergencies cluster at the two ends of it.

Before a session, or after a missed one, the patient is overloaded. Too much fluid, too much potassium. They are breathless, their legs are swollen, they cannot lie flat, and their chest sounds wet. It looks like heart failure and it is treated as a fluid problem. The potassium is the part you cannot see and cannot measure, and it causes fatal rhythm disturbances with very little warning. A patient who has missed two sessions is a fragile patient regardless of how they look.

After a session the problem reverses. Too much fluid has come off, or it came off too fast, and now the patient is hypotensive, cramping, dizzy, or has collapsed in the dialysis unit car park. Same patient, opposite problem, and the timing is what tells you which one you have.

So one question orients the entire call: when did you last dialyse? Before it, think overload. Just after it, think too much off. That single answer reframes everything you then find.

And the fistula rules stand, absolutely, on every dialysis call regardless of why you were sent. No blood pressure cuff on that arm. Nothing inserted into it. If it bleeds, firm sustained direct pressure and do not keep lifting it to check. That fistula is the patient's lifeline and clotting it off is a real injury, not a technicality.
read.standard: Renal failure impairs excretion of nitrogenous waste, fluid balance regulation and electrolyte homeostasis. Acute kidney injury develops over hours to days, commonly secondary to hypovolaemia, sepsis, hypoperfusion or nephrotoxic agents, and is frequently reversible. Chronic kidney disease is progressive and irreversible, ultimately requiring renal replacement therapy. Haemodialysis is typically performed three times weekly, each session removing accumulated fluid and solute. Emergencies cluster at either end of the dialysis interval. Pre-dialysis or following missed sessions, patients present with volume overload — dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, orthopnoea, pulmonary crackles — and hyperkalaemia, which produces fatal dysrhythmia without reliable prodrome and cannot be assessed prehospitally. Post-dialysis, excessive or overly rapid ultrafiltration produces hypotension, cramping, dizziness and syncope. Temporal relationship to the last session is the orienting historical question. Arteriovenous fistula precautions apply universally: no blood pressure measurement, no vascular access, and sustained direct pressure without release for haemorrhage.

eli_new.analogy: Dialysis is a tide that comes in over three days and goes out in four hours. The emergencies happen at high tide and at low tide, and the clock tells you which one you are looking at.
eli_new.body: One question does most of the work on any dialysis call: when did you last dialyse? Before it, they are probably too full. Just after it, they are probably too empty. The same patient produces opposite emergencies depending on where in the week you meet them.

concepts.title: Behavioral emergency assessment and scene safety
key_points: A behavioral emergency is behaviour the patient or those around them cannot manage, whatever its cause
Medical causes must be excluded before behaviour is called psychiatric: low blood sugar, hypoxia, head injury, infection, drugs and alcohol all present as behaviour change
Every behavioral patient gets a blood glucose and an oxygen saturation, without exception
Scene safety comes first and stays first: position yourself between the patient and the exit, never let yourself be cornered
Scan for potential weapons and note what is in reach, including ordinary objects
One person talks; the rest stay quiet. Multiple voices escalate an agitated patient
Speak calmly and slowly, give the patient space, avoid direct prolonged eye contact, and do not touch without warning
Never leave a behavioral patient alone, and never turn your back on one
misconceptions: Labelling behaviour psychiatric before checking a glucose
Standing between the patient and their own exit route so they feel trapped
Three crew members all talking at once
Approaching and touching an agitated patient without warning

read.plain:
A behavioral emergency is behaviour the patient cannot manage, or that the people around them cannot manage. That definition is deliberately broad, and it says nothing about cause — which is the whole point.

Because the most important thing in this concept is that behaviour is a symptom, and plenty of things that are not psychiatric produce it. Low blood sugar produces aggression. Hypoxia produces agitation and confusion. Head injuries produce combativeness. Infection produces delirium, especially in older people. Drugs and alcohol produce all of it. And every one of those has been written up as a psychiatric presentation by somebody who decided early.

So: a glucose and a saturation on every behavioral patient. Every one. It takes ninety seconds and it is the difference between a diagnosis and a label.

Now safety, which comes first and never stops being first.

Position yourself so you have a clear route out. Do not let yourself get backed into a bathroom, a bedroom, or the far end of a corridor. And here is the part people get wrong — do not block the patient's exit either. A frightened person who feels cornered fights. Both of you should be able to leave. In practice that usually means standing to one side rather than squarely in a doorway.

Look around as you come in. Not dramatically, just look. Kitchens have knives. Living rooms have heavy ornaments. Garages have tools. You are not being paranoid; you are noticing what is within reach so that you know before you need to.

One person talks. This is the single most useful thing a crew can do and it is broken constantly. When three people are asking questions, an agitated patient cannot process any of them and the volume in the room rises. Agree who is talking before you go in. Everybody else says nothing, stands still, and watches.

How you talk matters. Slow, quiet, short sentences. Leave more space than feels natural. Avoid long unbroken eye contact, which reads as a challenge. Tell them before you touch them, every time, and ask rather than announce where you can.

And two absolutes: never leave a behavioral patient on their own, and never turn your back on one. Not because they are dangerous by nature, but because you cannot see what you are not looking at, and the cost of being wrong is high.
read.standard: A behavioural emergency denotes behaviour the patient or their environment cannot manage, irrespective of aetiology. Organic causes must be excluded before psychiatric attribution: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, traumatic brain injury, infection and intoxication all produce behavioural disturbance. Blood glucose measurement and pulse oximetry are mandatory in every behavioural presentation. Scene safety is the initial and continuing priority: providers maintain unobstructed egress without obstructing the patient's own egress, as perceived entrapment escalates agitation. Environmental scanning for accessible weapons, including improvised objects, is performed on entry. Communication is conducted by a single designated provider, as multiple simultaneous speakers escalate agitated patients. Technique comprises slow quiet speech, short sentences, increased interpersonal distance, avoidance of sustained eye contact, and announcement prior to any physical contact. Behavioural patients are not left unattended and providers do not turn away from them.

eli_new.analogy: Behaviour is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Treating it as a diagnosis is the same mistake as treating a fever as a diagnosis.
eli_new.body: Two habits that separate crews who manage these calls well from crews who do not. First: check a sugar before you form an opinion. Second: decide in the ambulance who is going to talk, and then the other two genuinely say nothing.

concepts.title: Suicide risk assessment
key_points: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea — this is the single most important thing to know, and the fear of it stops people asking
Ask directly and plainly: are you thinking about killing yourself?
Risk rises with a specific plan, available means, a stated timeframe, and previous attempts
A previous attempt is one of the strongest predictors, so it is always asked about
Sudden calm after a period of severe distress can mean a decision has been made, not that the crisis has passed
Take every statement seriously, including ones that sound manipulative or attention-seeking
Remove or secure obvious means where it is safe to do so, and tell the receiving staff what was present
Do not leave the patient alone, and do not promise confidentiality you cannot keep
Document what the patient said in their own words
misconceptions: Not asking because it might give them the idea
Being reassured by sudden calm
Dismissing threats as attention-seeking
Promising not to tell anyone
exam_favorites: Asking directly does not plant the idea
Sudden calm as a warning sign

read.plain:
Start with the thing that stops people doing this properly: asking someone about suicide does not put the idea in their head. It does not increase risk. It is the single most persistent myth in this area and it stops crews asking the question that matters.

What asking actually does is give somebody permission to say out loud something they have been carrying alone, often for a long time. People are frequently relieved to be asked. Some will say yes to a stranger in a uniform when they have not been able to say it to anyone who loves them.

So ask, and ask plainly. Not 'you're not thinking of doing anything silly, are you' — which is a question shaped to get a no. Ask: are you thinking about killing yourself? Clear words, no euphemism, no apology for asking.

If the answer is yes, four things raise the risk.

A plan. Not just wanting to die, but having thought about how. The more specific it is, the more serious it is.

Means. Do they have access to what the plan requires? A plan with the means sitting in the next room is a different situation from a plan with no way to carry it out.

A timeframe. Tonight is different from someday.

And previous attempts. This is one of the strongest predictors there is, so always ask. Have you tried before? What happened?

Now the finding people misread. A patient who has been severely distressed and becomes suddenly calm and settled may not have recovered. That peace sometimes comes from having made a decision, and the relief of having decided. If a distressed patient becomes serene without anything having changed, that is a reason for more concern, not less.

Take everything seriously, including statements that feel manipulative. You cannot tell from the outside, the people who seem to be seeking attention sometimes die, and it is not your call to make. Treat the statement as real every time.

Practically: remove or secure obvious means where you safely can — the tablets on the table, the rope in the room — and tell the hospital what was there. Do not leave them alone, including in a toilet or while you fetch the trolley. And never promise to keep it secret, because you will pass this on, and a promise you break destroys the trust you needed.

Write down what they said in their own words. Their sentence, in quotation marks, is worth more than your summary of it.
read.standard: Enquiry regarding suicidal ideation does not induce or increase risk; this misconception is the principal barrier to assessment. Direct, unambiguous questioning is indicated. Risk stratification considers presence of a formulated plan, availability of means, specified timeframe, and history of previous attempts, the last constituting among the strongest predictors. Abrupt resolution of distress into calm may reflect decisional resolution rather than clinical improvement and warrants increased rather than decreased concern. All expressed ideation is treated as genuine irrespective of apparent secondary gain. Means are removed or secured where safe and reported to receiving staff. Patients are not left unattended, including during toileting. Confidentiality must not be promised. Documentation records patient statements verbatim.

eli_new.analogy: Asking is not handing someone a weapon. It is opening a door they have been standing behind.
eli_new.body: The two errors that matter. Not asking, because of a myth. And being reassured by a patient who has suddenly gone calm, when that calm can be the sound of a decision having been made.

concepts.title: Agitation, excited delirium and restraint principles
key_points: Severe agitation with a very high body temperature, extraordinary strength and apparent insensitivity to pain is a medical emergency, not simply a behavioural one
These patients die, and they die from the physiology — hyperthermia, exhaustion and acidosis — not from the behaviour
Sudden quiet after violent struggling is an ominous sign, not a sign that the patient has settled
Verbal de-escalation is attempted first and is often enough; restraint is a last resort
Restraint requires enough people to do it quickly and safely — too few people makes it more dangerous, not less
NEVER restrain a patient face down, and never hobble or hog-tie: positional asphyxia kills
A restrained patient is monitored continuously and never left unobserved, and the restraints are never used as a reason to stop assessing
Restrained patients still need a glucose, a saturation, a temperature and a full set of vital signs
Document why restraint was necessary, what was tried first, how many people, what type, and every reassessment
misconceptions: Restraining prone or hog-tying a patient
Reading sudden quiet after a struggle as the patient calming down
Restraining with too few people because waiting felt slow
Treating restraint as the end of assessment rather than the start of closer monitoring
Missing hyperthermia because everybody is focused on the struggle

read.plain:
Some agitated patients are not simply agitated. There is a presentation — variously named, and the naming is contested — of extreme agitation with a very high body temperature, remarkable strength, apparent insensitivity to pain, and a patient who cannot be reasoned with at all.

What you need to know about it is this: these patients die. And they die from physiology, not behaviour. Their temperature is dangerously high, they are in profound metabolic derangement from prolonged maximal exertion, and their body is being pushed past what it can sustain. It is a medical emergency dressed as a behavioural one, and treating it purely as a behaviour problem is how people end up dead in custody and on ambulance floors.

The most important single sign: sudden quiet after violent struggling. Everyone in the room exhales, because the fight is over and it feels like success. It is often the opposite. A patient who has been fighting at maximum effort and abruptly goes still may be arresting. If that happens, check — immediately, properly, pulse and breathing — do not stand back relieved.

De-escalation first, always, and it works more often than people expect. Time, quiet, space, one voice, and taking away whatever is making it worse. Many of these calls end without anybody touching anybody.

When restraint is genuinely necessary, some rules are absolute.

Enough people. Restraint with too few hands takes longer, involves more struggling, and hurts everybody — patient included. Waiting three minutes for enough people is safer than starting now with too few.

Never prone. Never face down, never hog-tied, never hobbled, never with a patient folded forward so they cannot expand their chest. Positional asphyxia is how restrained patients die, and it is entirely preventable. Supine or on the side, with the face visible and the chest free.

And once restrained, that patient needs more attention, not less. Continuous observation. Never out of sight. Check circulation in restrained limbs. And keep assessing — restraints are not a diagnosis, and a restrained patient still needs a blood glucose, an oxygen saturation, a temperature and a full set of vital signs. That temperature matters especially, because hyperthermia is the thing most likely to kill them and nobody takes a temperature while somebody is fighting.

Document properly: what the behaviour was, what you tried before restraint, why it became necessary, how many people were involved, what type of restraint, the position used, and every reassessment with times. This is the documentation most likely to be read carefully afterwards.
read.standard: Severe agitation accompanied by marked hyperthermia, apparent increased strength and diminished pain response constitutes a medical emergency; the terminology applied to this presentation is contested. Mortality derives from hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis and exhaustion consequent to sustained maximal exertion rather than from the behaviour itself. Abrupt cessation of struggling following violent resistance may indicate cardiorespiratory arrest and mandates immediate assessment rather than reassurance. Verbal de-escalation constitutes first-line management and is frequently sufficient. Where physical restraint is necessary, adequate personnel must be assembled; insufficient numbers prolong struggle and increase risk to all parties. Prone restraint, hobbling and hog-tying are absolutely contraindicated owing to positional asphyxia; supine or lateral positioning with the face visible and thorax unrestricted is required. Restrained patients require continuous observation, assessment of distal circulation, and complete vital signs including temperature, glucose and oxygen saturation. Documentation records the precipitating behaviour, de-escalation attempted, justification, personnel involved, restraint type and position, and all reassessments with times.

eli_new.analogy: A patient fighting at maximum effort is running an engine at redline. The danger is not the noise. It is what happens to the engine, and the silence when it stops.
eli_new.body: The moment that catches crews out is the moment of relief. Violent struggling stops, the room relaxes, and everybody takes a breath. That is precisely when you should be checking a pulse.

He had been struggling at full effort for several minutes and was drenched and burning hot to touch.

concepts.title: Legal aspects of psychiatric transport
key_points: Competent adults may refuse care, and mental illness alone does not remove that capacity
Capacity is about whether this patient can understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision about this particular issue, now
Capacity can fluctuate and is decision-specific: someone may have capacity for one choice and not another
Implied consent covers a patient who cannot consent and is in an emergency
Legal frameworks exist for involuntary transport of patients who are a danger to themselves or others, and they differ by jurisdiction — know yours
Involuntary transport usually requires law enforcement or a designated official, not an EMT acting alone
Transporting an adult with capacity against their will can constitute assault or false imprisonment
Document the capacity assessment, what the patient was told, what they said, who was present, and the legal authority relied on
When it is genuinely unclear, involve medical direction and law enforcement rather than deciding alone
misconceptions: Assuming a psychiatric diagnosis means the patient cannot refuse
Transporting an adult with capacity against their will
Relying on family consent for a competent adult
Deciding alone in an ambiguous case rather than seeking direction
exam_favorites: Mental illness does not remove capacity

read.plain:
This is the area where good intentions cause legal problems, so it is worth being precise.

A competent adult can refuse medical care. All of it. Even when the refusal is unwise, even when it will harm them, even when everybody in the room disagrees. That right does not disappear because somebody has a psychiatric diagnosis. A person with schizophrenia, depression or bipolar disorder can have full capacity, and frequently does.

Capacity is not a global label. It is about this decision, at this moment. Four things: can the person understand the information, retain it long enough to use it, weigh it up against alternatives, and communicate their decision? All four, for this specific decision, now.

And it moves. Somebody may have capacity this hour and not the next. Someone may have capacity to decide about a dressing and not about a life-threatening refusal. So it is assessed for the decision in front of you, not established once and filed away.

Where a patient cannot consent — unconscious, or without capacity — and there is an emergency, implied consent covers acting in their best interests. That is the default position and it exists precisely so that nobody stands and watches.

Every jurisdiction has a legal mechanism for transporting somebody involuntarily when they pose a danger to themselves or to others. The names, the criteria and the paperwork differ enormously between systems. You have to know yours, specifically, and knowing it in general terms is not enough.

What is nearly universal is that an EMT does not invoke it alone. Involuntary transport normally requires law enforcement, a physician, or another designated official depending on the system. If you are considering moving an adult against their will, somebody else with that authority should be involved.

The risk of getting it wrong runs both ways, and both are serious. Transporting a competent adult against their will can be assault and false imprisonment. Leaving a patient who lacked capacity, and who then comes to harm, is abandonment. Neither is a comfortable place to be, which is exactly why the documentation matters.

So write it down properly: your assessment of capacity and what you based it on, what you told the patient about the risks, what they said back — in their words — who else was present, and what legal authority you relied on if the transport was involuntary.

And when it is genuinely unclear, it is not your decision to make alone. Medical direction, law enforcement, and if your service has one, a mental health professional. Calling for help with a difficult decision is not weakness; it is what the system is for.
read.standard: Adults with decision-making capacity may refuse care irrespective of the apparent wisdom of that refusal; psychiatric diagnosis does not itself negate capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and temporally variable, requiring that the patient understand relevant information, retain it, weigh it against alternatives, and communicate a decision. Implied consent applies where a patient lacks capacity and an emergency exists, permitting treatment in the patient's best interests. Statutory mechanisms for involuntary transport of patients posing danger to self or others exist in all jurisdictions but differ substantially in criteria, terminology and procedure; providers must know local provisions specifically. Invocation ordinarily requires law enforcement, a physician or another designated authority rather than the EMT alone. Transport of a capacitous adult against their will may constitute assault and false imprisonment; failure to transport an incapacitous patient who subsequently suffers harm may constitute abandonment. Documentation records the capacity assessment and its basis, information given, patient responses verbatim, persons present, and the legal authority relied upon. Ambiguous cases warrant consultation with medical direction and law enforcement.

eli_new.analogy: Capacity is a key cut for one lock at one moment, not a passport that works everywhere forever.
eli_new.body: The instinct when someone is unwell and refusing help is to take them anyway because you are trying to help. That instinct is how EMTs end up in legal trouble. The answer is not to abandon the patient — it is to bring in the people who have the authority you do not.

story.title: He said no
story.dispatch: Medic 1 — 28-year-old male, family report he has stopped his medication.
story.body:
He answered the door, listened to everything the crew said, repeated the risks back to them accurately, and said he was not going to hospital today.

His mother was distressed and asked them to just take him. The crew explained, more than once, that they could not.

He had a diagnosis. He also understood, retained, weighed and communicated. Those are different things, and only the second one decides.
